utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then I will proceed. May it please the Court. Good morning again to the members of the distinguished panel, and good morning to my colleagues on the other side of the aisle with the Prosecution. As you know, the matter before you is an appeal of a judgement handed down against my client, Anto Furundzija, on 10 December 1998. The appeal before you raises fundamental issues of justice and human rights, and it will be your duty in this case to ensure that basic internationally guaranteed civil and human rights are protected at the International Tribunal. You five Judges have been given a mandate by the Security Council to ensure that the trials conducted at the ICTY are in accordance with minimum guarantees of international human rights as found in Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights, customary International Law, and last, but certainly not least, the Statute of the Tribunal. Your Honours, in creating the International Tribunal, the Security Council took into consideration the fact that Trial Chambers and Trial Judges are not infallible. That is the reason that the Security Council, in Article 11, authorised the creation of an Appeals Chamber in order to ensure that mistakes made at the trial level could be corrected on appeal. In the practice of the ICTY, we have already seen that this was a wise decision, as the Appellate Chamber has already acted to overturn the Trial Chambers in at least two cases, Tadic and Erdemovic. You, the Trial Chamber, are now being asked to review the judgements in this case. You five Judges have been charged by the Security Council to be the guardians of Article 6 of the European Convention, Article 14 of the International Covenant, and the Statute. You are the five individuals who will determine whether the rights enumerated in these conventions and international covenants, as well as the Statute, are simply hurdles and obstacles to be overcome in pursuant of criminal convictions or which, when defended on behalf of one man, such an Anto Furundzija, are defended for all of us all over the world. I submit to you, Your Honours, that you are called in this case to defend the rights defined in these international covenants and conventions, not just for Anto Furundzija but for every current and future defendant at the ICTY, at the ICTR, the future ICC, and in domestic jurisdictions around the world. You are asked or, better said, you are duty-bound to protect the fundamental right to a fair trial. In the case before you, I do not believe that any reasonable person could contend that Mr. Furundzija received a fair trial. At the end of the day and when you retire to your Chambers to deliberate your opinion, you will have no doubt that Mr. Furundzija's fundamental rights to a fair trial were violated in several ways. First and foremost, he not only did not receive fair notice of the charges against him, but he was affirmatively misled by both the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber as to the facts and charges against him. Where a defendant is affirmatively misled, both before and during trial, so as not to know the nature and charges against him, he cannot be deemed to have received a fair trial. Second, the Trial Chamber ignored in its judgement critical exculpatory evidence which raised more than a reasonable doubt as to the Trial Chamber's most critical finding in this case. Specifically, the Trial Chamber's judgement turns on the pivotal finding that during the course of a rape and sexual assault being committed by a co-accused in a room which came to be known in this trial as the pantry, Mr. Furundzija was conducting an interrogation of the victim. As will be demonstrated later in my argument, this conclusion completely ignored clear and convincing evidence to the contrary, that Mr. Furundzija did not question anyone in the pantry during a rape, or sexual assault, or any other assault. This was told to the Trial Chamber not by a Defence witness but by a Prosecution witness. Remarkably, the Trial Chamber did not consider or address this testimony in its judgement and then proceeded to not only convict Mr. Furundzija but sentenced him to a harsh sentence of ten years imprisonment on the basis of this factual finding. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber ignored exculpatory evidence that certainly, at the very least, creates a reasonable doubt as to Mr. Furundzija's guilt. As the guardians of the right to a fair trial, you five Judges must correct this injustice and reverse the convictions. Preliminarily, I think it's important that we address first what the standard of review is for this Appeals Chamber on appeal. The standard of review in this Chamber must necessarily take into account the standard of review in the Trial Chamber. That is, this Appellate Chamber must have the authority to go back and review the evidence to determine whether or not a reasonable doubt existed at trial. Part of our authority that we rely on comes, in fact, from the Tadic appeal, which was decided in July of last year. There, the Appeals Chamber determined whether or not the standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt was correctly applied, except in that case it was the Prosecutor appealing that there was no reasonable doubt. Regardless, now that it is a defendant that is appealing that, the same principle applies. The Trial Chamber has the authority to review whether the standard was correctly applied. The test for proof beyond a reasonable doubt is as follows: The evidence must be so overwhelming that it excludes every fair or rational hypothesis except that of guilt. That is, a conviction requires the absence of any reasonable hypothesis that can be derived from the evidence other than guilt. If there was any rational hypothesis at trial that Mr. Furundzija was not guilty of these charges, then the Trial Chamber was required to accept that hypothesis under the standard of "beyond a reasonable doubt." Mr. Furundzija thus appeals on the basis that the Trial Chamber was unreasonable in concluding that the only fair or rational hypothesis that could be derived from the evidence is that Mr. Furundzija is guilty. In fact, it is clear from the evidence that there were fair and rational hypotheses in the evidence of Mr. Furundzija's innocence which required the Trial Chamber to acquit my client. What do the reported cases indicate an Appellate Chamber must do on appeal? The first principle is that the Appellate Chamber has the right and the obligation to conduct its own independent assessment of the evidence, both as to its sufficiency and as to its quality. After independently reviewing this evidence, the Appellate Chamber must then determine whether or not the Trial Chamber ought to have entertained a reasonable doubt as to the guilt of the defendant. In short, the Appellate Chamber must determine whether the Trial Chamber, acting reasonably, should have found that there is a fair and rational inference of innocence in the evidence. If so, the defendant's conviction must be reversed. The Prosecution, in its appellate brief, argues for a standard which says that if there is any basis in the evidence to conclude that the Trial Chamber's conclusion was reasonable, then the Appellate Chamber cannot overturn that decision. We propose, Your Honours, first, that that position is inconsistent with what the Appellate Chamber did in the Tadic appeal in ruling in favour of the Prosecution. Second, it's inconsistent with -- the very standard which I have enumerated here is inconsistent with the position they took in the Tadic appeal, according, at least, to the written decision. And third, to not allow an Appellate Chamber to go back and review whether there was a reasonable doubt would, in effect, preclude a defendant from an effective right to an appeal. If at trial the defendant is entitled to be acquitted if there is a reasonable doubt, then he is entitled to argue at the appellate level if there was a reasonable doubt. Indeed, under the Prosecution standard, at least as I understand it, the defendant only gets one chance to argue that there was reasonable doubt, and that is at the trial level. And then the Appellate Chamber is precluded from doing its own review as to whether or not there is a reasonable doubt. Again, that is contrary, I believe, to the precedent already set in Tadic and contrary to the overwhelming weight of law in domestic jurisdictions. Finally on that issue, here is the best way I can articulate this. The standard is as follows: Even if the Trial Chamber were to retire and find that the defendant probably did it, but they were also to find that there is, however, a reasonable argument that could be made on the evidence that he didn't, then the Trial Chamber, and now the Appellate Chamber, must acquit him, because despite the fact that the defendant probably did it, if there is that reasonable hypothesis that can be derived from the evidence of innocence, then he must be acquitted. And that is the standard that must be applied at the trial levels here, and also on the appellate level. The Appellate Chamber should keep in mind that once the defendant presents, through direct examination or cross-examination, a Defence, the fundamental presumption of innocence, until proven guilty, precludes the trier of fact from simply ignoring the exculpatory evidence. And if there is any reasonable hypothesis consistent with evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise again to the people in the booth. Thus, if Mr. Furundzija, through Witness D in this case, introduced evidence that he did not interrogate anyone in the pantry, it must have been accepted. The fact that the Trial Chamber did not, requires this Appellate Chamber to act by reversing the judgement of the Trial Chamber. Throughout this appeal, then, Your Honours, I will be using that standard, and that is that I will demonstrate now through the evidence that there in fact were fair and rational hypotheses that could have been derived from the evidence of innocence. I think at this time I would like to ask the Registrar to assist me here. But I would like to take a few moments to first establish exactly what the Trial Chamber found in the judgement, so that we all know what exactly we are talking about. Your Honours, I will be using the board, but you will each have a copy in front of you, as will the Prosecution, of the board itself, to make it easier for you to read and follow. In brief, first, I am sure you've read the briefs, but I will -- the case was about a series of incidents that happened to one woman, starting on or about May 15 of 1993. The allegations in the indictment, and which were ultimately found in the judgement, were that this woman was brought to a place called "the Bungalow" in Nadioci, and then taken out behind to a weekend house next to the Bungalow. The allegations, in short, were -- at least that everyone can agree on, that she was raped and sexually assaulted in two different rooms in this weekend house. One came to be known at trial as the large room, and is referred to as such in the judgement. And the second came to be known as the pantry. The events in the large room temporally happened first, and then the events in the pantry followed. So first I am going to discuss what the Trial Chamber found with respect to what happened in the large room. The Trial Chamber found as follows. And I have paragraph numbers indicating where in the judgement you can find this. The first finding of fact that's important is that when Witness A was taken to the weekend house, that she was brought into this large room, and that immediately upon her arrival, or just shortly thereafter, Mr. Furundzija arrived and appeared in the room, where he immediately commenced an interrogation of Witness A. According to the judgement, during this interrogation, at some point Witness A gave an answer, and that from behind her, for the first time, appears Accused B. He puts a knife to her throat and makes an oral threat to her, while she is in front of Mr. Furundzija being interrogated. Furundzija commenced the interrogation of the -- I'm sorry, this is in this first part where he commenced the interrogation without Accused B. Then Accused B arrived. After questioned by Furundzija, Accused B grabbed Witness A by the hair, put a knife to her throat, then forced her to undress and remove her glasses. Again, all of this is in front of Mr. Furundzija, according to the judgement. Paragraph 82, Furundzija continues with the interrogation of Witness A. Witness A is forced to remain naked in front of approximately 40 soldiers. Accused B then -- again, all this is in front of Mr. Furundzija -- drew a knife over Witness A's body and thighs, threatening to cut out her private parts. Furundzija allegedly continued the interrogation while this is happening. The final finding, at least with respect to Mr. Furundzija, is paragraph 83. Furundzija becomes annoyed and threatens Witness A to make her confess by confronting her with Witness D. Furundzija leaves Witness A in the room, and then another phase of serious sexual assaults by Accused B, accompanied by questioning, follows. From these facts, the Trial Chamber makes several conclusions, and it's said in the judgement. "The Trial Chamber is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that: A, Witness A was interrogated by the accused in the large room; B, she was forced by Accused B to undress and remain naked before a substantial number of soldiers," which from the judgement you can determine includes Mr. Furundzija. "C, she was subjected to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment and to threats of physical assault by Accused B in the course of her interrogation by the accused; D, the interrogation by the accused, and the abuse by Accused B, were parallel to each other. Witness A was left by the accused in the custody of Accused B, who proceeded to rape her, sexually assault her, and to physically abuse and degrade her." Although the conclusion is not stated, a reasonable reading of this makes it appear that Mr. Furundzija knowingly left this woman in the custody of Accused B, knowing that she was going to be -- continue to be abused, up to and including rape. The next room is the pantry, and that is Exhibit A2. Now, what happens after Witness A is raped by accused B outside the presence of Furundzija, Witness A is taken to the pantry, and there she was confronted with Witness D. Witness A says Furundzija interrogated her with -- interrogated Witness A with Witness D in the pantry. When Accused B started to beat Witness D, Witness A says Furundzija was in the doorway. Witness D says Furundzija was outside the room with other soldiers. At this point later on I will -- you can start to see where the conflict starts in the testimony. But I'll continue. Paragraph 87 says: "The attacks then turned to Witness A. Accused B hit Witness A, forcing her to perform oral sex on him, and raped her. Witness D was forced to watch. Then this inference from the Trial Chamber. "It appears to the Trial Chamber that the accused would have had to be in the vicinity of the door in order for Witness D to have seen him amidst the group of soldiers. Witness A stated that Furundzija was there all the time. 266. "The Trial Chamber finds the accused was also present in the pantry where the second phase of Witness A's interrogation occurred. Both Witness A and Witness D were interrogated by the accused and hit on the feet with the baton by Accused B during questioning in the pantry. Accused B again assaulted Witness A, who was still naked, before the other soldiers." And this again is the pivotal factual finding in the case. "The accused continued to interrogate Witness A in the same manner as he had done earlier in the large room. As the interrogation intensified, so did the sexual assault and the rape." There can be no doubt that that is the pivotal finding. Paragraph 87. "Witness D says that when he was taken out of the pantry, he saw the accused outside the doorway." Paragraph 270. "The Trial Chamber --" and this confirms again that pivotal factual finding. "The Trial Chamber has found that Witness A was subjected to rape and sexual assaults by Accused B in the course of the interrogation by the accused. There is no doubt that the accused, and Accused B, as commanders, divided the process of interrogation by performing different functions. The role of the accused was to question, while accused B's role was to assault and threaten in order to elicit the required information from Witness A and Witness D." Then finally: "The Trial Chamber finds that in relation to Witness A, the elements of torture have been met. Within the provisions of Article 7(1) and the findings of the Trial Chamber on the liability for torture ..." Now, I have emphasised this. "... the accused is a co-perpetrator by virtue of his interrogation of her as integral to that torture." So it is not that he was present or may have been present; it is that his interrogation is an integral part of that torture. "The Trial Chamber, therefore, finds beyond reasonable doubt that whilst naked, but covered with a blanket, Witness A was interrogated by the accused in the pantry. Witness A was subjected to rape, sexual assaults, and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment by Accused B." Here they insert Witness D, which I will discuss later. "Witness D was also interrogated by the accused and subjected to serious physical assaults by Accused B. Witness D was made to watch rape and sexual assault perpetrated upon a woman whom he knew in order to force him to admit allegations made against her. In this regard both witnesses were humiliated." And finally: "Accused B beat Witness D and repeatedly raped Witness A. The accused was present in the room as he carried on his interrogations. When not in the room, he was present in the near vicinity just outside an open door, and he knew that crimes, including rape, were being committed." In fact, the acts by Accused B were performed in pursuant of the accused's interrogation. Your Honours, those are the critical facts of the judgement. Now I will proceed to explain to you why all of those conclusions are not sustainable by the evidence. I'm going to turn to the first issue on appeal, and that is whether Anto Furundzija was given fair notice of the charges to be proven against him in violation of Articles 20 and 21(4) of the Statute of the Tribunal. I think that each member of the Appellate Chamber will agree with the proposition that an accused's right to fair notice of the nature and cause of the charges against him is fundamental to his right to a fair trial. The commentary to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights states that the term "nature and cause of the charge" means not only the exact legal description of the offence but also the facts underlying it. If the Prosecutor and the Trial Chamber not only failed to inform Mr. Furundzija of the facts underlying the charges against him but also patently misled him as to the nature of the charges against him, this Appellate Chamber must reverse the Trial Chamber's convictions. One of the key documents in this case, as in any case, is the indictment. What does an indictment do? It identifies the charges against the defendant, it identifies the facts supporting these charges, including but not limited to the identity of the victim, the approximate date of the alleged offence, the means by which the offence was committed, and the material facts upon which the Prosecution relies must be pleaded, as well as the defendant's particular course of conduct. Thus, the indictment defines but also at the same time limits the criminal case against the accused. It is this document which is meant to implement and satisfy a defendant's right to notice under the relevant international covenants and agreements. It is this document upon which the defendant must, out of necessity, rely in preparing his defence against the charges. For this reason, a prosecutor, not just here but anywhere, cannot seek a conviction on the basis of material facts which are not pleaded in the indictment. Oftentimes, a prosecutor will be faced with many different scenarios of the facts of the case prior to filing an indictment. However, the necessity of an indictment requires that a prosecutor determines which of those factual situations they intend to choose. They choose that factual situation, and then they submit it in the form of an indictment in this case to the Trial Chamber for confirmation. Then the Prosecutor must live with that choice unless they exercise their rights under Rule 50 and file to amend the indictment. If this is not the case, then there is no reason for an indictment or for a procedure amending an indictment, if the Prosecutor is not bound by the submissions made in that document. For this reason, because this is one of our fundamental issues of appeal, I'm going to go over exactly what happened at the pre-trial stage here in terms of what the indictment actually alleges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In examining the indictment, the indictment in this case is against four accused. One is Mr. Furundzija. The remaining three are still under seal, but it is clear that one of the accused is Accused B. The indictment is divided into several different periods of time involving several different acts. Counts 1 through 8 do not involve Witness A, and it appears to me that they involve Accused B's conduct with respect to other individuals at other times. Now, at count 9 is where the indictment starts to examine what happened to Witness A, and in the indictment what happened to Witness A is divided into three different segments. Counts 9 through 11 are the large room. These are the counts that relate to when Witness A was first taken to the weekend house by the Bungalow. Counts 12 through -- and I'm sorry; I might add, do not involve Mr. Furundzija. Counts 12 through 14 involve, in paragraph 25, a brief moment in the large room at the end of all of these events, and then the pantry incident. And there it's Furundzija and Accused B. After count 14, if you will recall from the facts of this case, counts 9 through 14 happened in one day; they are the large room and the pantry. Witness A, however, was held in captivity by Accused B for approximately ten weeks following this incident, so counts, I believe, 17 or 18 through 23 deal with that ten-week period subsequent to what happened in the weekend house. So we have three different time periods. We have counts 9 through 11 for the large room, counts 12 through 14 for the pantry, and then an additional several counts for that ten-week period where she was held in captivity. What do counts 9 through 11 allege? On or about 15 May, Witness A was taken to a building called the Bungalow. There Accused B, in front of other soldiers, forced Witness A to remove her clothing, caressed her body with a knife, threatened to kill her, and told her that all the men who were present in the room would rape her. Then Accused B forced Witness A to dance naked. Paragraph 24. Accused B next proceeded to rape Witness A by forcing her to perform oral sex and to swallow his sperm and urine. Accused B forced Witness A to have sexual intercourse with him, both vaginally and anally. Accused B penetrated Witness A's mouth, vagina and anus with his penis. During these incidents, Accused B bit -- I'm sorry, Accused B bit Witness A about the body, including on her nipples. Accused B forced Witness A to commit these acts with him several times, so there are several rapes that occur in the large room. During these rapes, Accused B rubbed his knife on Witness A's body and put his revolver in her mouth and against her forehead. Then it says, "By the foregoing acts and omissions, Accused B committed the following crimes," and then it lists them; count 9 for a grave breach, count 10 for torture, and count 11 for outrages upon personal dignity, including rape. So it is clear from the indictment that there was a series of rapes and sexual assaults that occurred in the large room prior to Mr. Furundzija's alleged arrival. Why? Because we turn to count 12, and it says: "On or about 15 May, shortly after the events described in paragraphs 21 and 22," and this is a typo, because it should be "23" and "24," since 21 and 22 have nothing to do with Witness A, "at the Jokers' headquarters, Anto Furundzija, the local commander of the Jokers, and another soldier interrogated Witness A." Again, the key clause is "shortly after the events described in these paragraphs." What does paragraph 25 allege with respect to the criminal conduct of Anto Furundzija? It says: "While being questioned by Furundzija, Accused B rubbed his knife against Witness A's inner thigh and lower stomach and threatened to put his knife inside Witness A's vagina should she not tell the truth." So the criminal allegations here in this paragraph are that Mr. Furundzija conducted an interrogation of Witness A when then Accused B made an oral threat and made physical contact with a knife. And the issue for the Trial Chamber at trial was, "Does that conduct rise to the level of torture?" Twenty-six, this is the pantry paragraph. Then Witness A and Victim B, who at trial came to be known as Witness D, a Bosnian Croat who had previously assisted Witness A's family, were taken to another room in the Bungalow, the pantry. Victim B had been badly beaten prior to this time. While Furundzija continued to interrogate Witness A and Victim B, again Witness D, Accused B beat Witness A and Victim B on the feet with a baton. Then Accused B forced Witness A to have oral and vaginal sexual intercourse with him. Furundzija was present during this entire incident and did nothing to stop or curtail Accused B's actions. So what are the charges here? Furundzija then went to the pantry where A and D were located. While he then proceeded to interrogate both A and D, Accused B is alleged to have assaulted A and D with a baton, and then the allegation is that Furundzija is present when the next phase began, which is the sexual assault of Witness A. "By the foregoing acts and omissions, Accused B and Anto Furundzija committed the following crimes," and then it's "torture as a grave breach," which was, as you know, withdrawn by the Prosecution; count 13, for torture, and count 14, for an outrage upon personal dignity, including rape. There are no allegations of a conspiracy between Accused B and Mr. Furundzija, no allegation of a concert of action, and no allegation of forced nudity, at least with respect to Mr. Furundzija. Why? Because the indictment alleges that a whole series of rapes and sexual assaults happened prior to Mr. Furundzija's arrival, again shortly after the events described in these paragraphs. And it's important to note that at the time that the indictment was filed in 1995, the only witness statement that the Prosecution had from Witness A was her 1995 witness statement which was taken by Brenda Hollis and another Tribunal investigator. The entire indictment is based on that one statement, and it is that statement that was submitted to the reviewing Judge for confirmation. This indictment is consistent with that statement. You will also note, Your Honours, that there is no allegation at any point in time that Anto Furundzija left Witness A in the custody of Accused B, where she was subsequently raped. Why? Because those rapes in the indictment happened temporally before Mr. Furundzija arrived on the scene. Hence, he didn't leave her there, because under the allegations in the indictment, that wasn't the way the case was pleaded. Again, after count 14, Anto Furundzija allegedly is not on the scene anymore. The remaining defendants in those counts are charged with torture, rape and unlawful confinement of Witness A for the subsequent weeks of her ordeal. It is thus clear, Your Honours, that it is the Prosecutor in 1995 that divided these events into three separate periods, 9 to 11, 12 to 14, and then the 10-week period, and then the additional counts that deal with it after that. As we proceeded to trial, I want to demonstrate for the Appellate Chamber just how much the Defence was relying on the indictment, which is what we are supposed to do and is the only thing we can rely on. On April 6th I filed, on Mr. Furundzija's behalf, a motion to dismiss this indictment. I filed it on the basis that under the authority in the Tadic case with respect to torture -- or aiding and abetting, I'm sorry -- the standard is that the aider and abettor must provide direct and substantial assistance to the perpetrator in order to be convicted for aiding and abetting. So in the motion to dismiss of April 6, I argued that, as a matter of law, without even having to go to trial, I wanted the Trial Chamber to review whether, as a matter of law, Mr. Furundzija could be convicted of direct and substantial assistance where Accused B, by the very indictment itself, is alleged to have committed at least four rapes prior to Mr. Furundzija's arrival. He continues a rape in the pantry and then holds Witness A captive for 10 weeks, where he continually rapes and sexually assaults her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, it may help my colleagues and me on the Bench to follow you a little more closely if you did this. You are now addressing us on a motion to dismiss the indictment. Would you like to relate this to a particular ground of appeal? There are six grounds, I believe. Which one are you now busy with?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is still on the fair notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Fair notice. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is the fair notice issue. And what I am trying to demonstrate to the Trial Chamber is our reliance on the indictment and how -- I'm not arguing the motion itself. That isn't at issue here. What is at issue is to demonstrate to the Appellate Chamber that the defendant and his counsel relied on the fact that this is what the Prosecution had pleaded, namely, that these rapes had taken place prior to Mr. Furundzija's arrival. Ultimately, the Trial Chamber denied our motion. But my point to you is that this was still going to be an issue at trial for us, and we were preparing for trial. And one of the bases for the Defence was going to be the very fact that, in closing argument, we were going to argue it can't be direct and substantial assistance where this Accused B engaged in this criminal conduct several times before, and then for 10 weeks after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Don't by any means allow me to divert you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is as much for you as it is for me. So if at any time I -- I appreciate when you interject whenever something is unclear to you, and I look forward to answering your questions. So I would ask all of the members of the Appellate Chamber to do the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I am trying to follow you. You say the incidents in counts 9 to 11, in the large room, took place when Mr. Furundzija was not there, but in counts 12 to 14, paragraph 26, there was a rape, allegedly, in his presence a rape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. What I am trying to show is Your Honours -- and I will demonstrate a couple of more things. But to answer that, yes, you are correct, but the rape he is alleged to have been present for is the rape that happened in the pantry. So in preparing for trial, here is what we thought the issues in the case were: A, whether -- first we were going to argue that she wasn't credible, because we deny that this incident ever took place, but even assuming that the Trial Chamber were to find that it did with respect to this oral threat and the rubbing of the knife, we were going to make a legal argument also that this doesn't rise to the level of torture. Then with respect to paragraph 26. That is where Witness A and Witness D are allegedly confronted in the pantry and Witness A is raped in Mr. Furundzija's presence. So we do not appeal on the basis that we didn't have fair notice of that charge. What we are appealing is, if you look back on what the Trial Chamber found in the large room, and you will see that as we go on, the Trial Chamber went back in the judgement and put Mr. Furundzija from here and put him here [indicating]. And it said that he started the interrogation, if you recall. And that's why I went through this with the Appellate Chamber first. He started the interrogation, and then when he was questioning, that's when Accused B first arrives on the scene.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, we have another call from the translators. You've heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- I apologise. As I will demonstrate later, Judge Robinson, the argument that we have, then, is that all of these conclusions about concert of action, about that Furundzija was the interrogator from the start, about leaving her in the room, where she was subsequently raped by Accused B, all of those things, as a matter of law, are impossible if -- if the Trial Chamber -- I'm sorry. If the Prosecution had proved this case at trial, then the judgement would, as a matter of law, would not have been able to be -- would not have been lawful. Had the Prosecution proved this case, they could not have proved the judgement at trial. And I don't know if you follow me on that, but the fact of the matter is all of these things are alleged to have happened before Furundzija's arrival, and then he appears. And if you read the judgement or the two exhibits I started off with, that's not what the Trial Chamber found. Here again is A1. This is the large room. This is what the judgement says, ultimately. Furundzija in the room before Accused B. Furundzija commenced the interrogation without Accused B. Then B arrives. Then B grabs her by the hair, puts a knife to her throat, and forces her to undress. Furundzija continues to interrogate Witness A while all of this is going on. Well, under the indictment that's impossible. And more importantly, this is what we prepared the Defence on. He is convicted on this, on the large room. He is convicted on 12 and 14, but on the basis of allegations that are in 9 through 11, as well as 12 through 14. And if you note, for all of this conduct, Accused B was facing six counts; right. Furundzija is facing three. So by the very way that the indictment is separated, B's conduct is more severe and requires more sanction than Furundzija's, at least as alleged in the indictment. And it is from this basic document, as I said, that we then, as his lawyers, prepare the case. And the case is all of this happens, then Furundzija arrives at the end of this, then this happens in the pantry. So that's what we prepared for trial on. I think, in a couple of moments, this argument will be even more clear. While we are doing this -- I don't need to use those to explain something else. On that motion to dismiss that I was talking about earlier, the Court set an oral argument on that motion for the 29th of April, and at that hearing again the Trial Chamber denied the motion. But this is what Judge May told me, because I also made more arguments -- I had made an argument that we still did not know the factual bases of the allegations. So here is what Judge May said to me directly, and I quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, would you just help me on one point. Possibly I wasn't following you as closely as I ought to have done. The document which is marked A4, you have a paragraph 25 at the top. And in lines 2 and 3, I read this: "On or about 15 May 1993, shortly after the events described in," I think you said, "paragraphs 23 and 24 (sic)" et cetera. Now, those words do not seem to appear in paragraph 25 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think what you are looking at is the amended --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I am going to get to that at the moment. But what happened was -- and if you allow me to finish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then I will not anticipate you. I will allow you to reach it in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just make a note of that, so I don't forget. Again, to go back to that hearing. Judge May said the following to me: "It is clearly right that you have all of the material before the trial so that you can prepare for it properly, and also right that you know the way in which the Prosecutor puts the case, how do they put the case against your client, how do they say that he was involved in these offences. All that is clearly so, and in due course we will find out." The due course that Judge May is referring to there is that the Trial Chamber agreed with our argument that this indictment still was too vague. So they ordered the Prosecution to file by May 1 a document which would specify the charges for the defendant as he prepares for trial. And they did so. And then, I believe about three weeks later, the Prosecutor had to file their pre-trial brief. So they made more factual assertions about what they intended to prove at trial. I think it was filed on the 22nd of May, so about 22 days after they filed this pleading in response to a Trial Chamber order. So now, as you know, I have indicated that our reliance was on the fact that several assaults and rapes had happened in the first room. We get the Prosecutor's reply, and it says -- I'll skip the first paragraph: "Witness A was taken to a house behind the Bungalow and waited for the boss to appear. One man, Accused B, forced Witness A to undress, whereby he repeatedly sexually assaulted her and threatened her with a knife and a revolver." Okay. Key paragraph: "After this, after this, the accused, Anto Furundzija, came into the room and said to Witness A, who was still in a state of forced nudity, 'Now, lady, interrogation period.' And then he rubbed his knife on the inside of her thigh and lower stomach and threatened her again orally. "Then the accused and Accused B and another Joker removed Witness A to an adjacent room that she refers to as the pantry. Witness D was then brought into this room. Furundzija continued his line of questioning while Accused B beat both Witness A and Witness D on their feet with a baton." The point is, now on this May 1 document, our reading of the indictment is absolutely confirmed. Several events, i.e. 9 through 11 against Accused B in the indictment, happened before Furundzija arrives. After this the accused, Anto Furundzija, came in. So our theory about direct and substantial assistance, which is something we intended to prove at trial -- something we intended to show at trial and argue, was still clearly relevant because they are continuing to allege that something happened before. In their pre-trial brief, again the same thing: "Witness A was taken to the barracks, located behind the Bungalow, where she was forced to dance nude in front for the soldiers and then was threatened with a knife and then repeatedly sexually abused by a member of the unit. "Anto Furundzija, the local commander, arrived and immediately began to interrogate Witness A, even though she was in a state of nudity. While being questioned by Anto Furundzija, the other soldier ..." and here is the key again "... who had previously raped Witness A." So again, confirmation of the indictment, confirmation of the May 1 pleading. And now, approximately 15 days before trial, we get the pre-trial brief, where we are told this is what they are going to allege. This is their theory of the case. Accused B shows up, rapes her repeatedly, sexually assaults her. At that point Anto Furundzija is alleged to have arrived. As I stated earlier, this is entirely consistent with the 1995 witness statement of Witness A, upon which the indictment was initially based. And then it continues on, that they were then taken to the pantry, where then Furundzija conducted this interrogation in the pantry of both D and A, and that the rape and sexual assault then transpired in his presence. So how are we preparing for trial as the Defence? All we can do is look at the indictment, we go to the Trial Chamber several times prior to trial and say, "We need more facts to prepare this case." The Trial Chamber agrees, grants our motion, orders them to specify the facts, because we are entitled to rely on the facts and know the facts before trial. We get that document. They then, for the third time, 15 days before trial, affirm their theory of the case. So what happens then? Witness D was obviously a critical witness in this case. I will tell the Appellate Chamber that the Defence made every effort to find Witness D, because obviously he has extremely relevant information as to Mr. Furundzija's guilt or innocence. No one could find him. I found him, but he wouldn't talk to me, I should say. So we were left to do what we had to do at trial. About the time that the Prosecutor files the pre-trial brief, which is 15 days or so before trial, the Prosecutor locates Witness D, for the first time. The Prosecutor takes the statement of Witness D and Witness D's -- Witness D's statement says: "I know for sure that during the time that rapes and sexual assaults occurred in the pantry by Accused B, I know for sure that Anto Furundzija was not present in the room." Obviously, when we got that witness statement, Your Honour, about 10 days before trial, we were very interested in calling Witness D as a Defence witness, because that information, to us, is the heart of the case, the allegation that Mr. Furundzija interrogated A and D while they were being raped, and now here D gives a statement to the Prosecutor where he says Furundzija wasn't present in the room. So what happens in this 10-day period between that pre-trial brief and the opening of the trial on the 8th of June? Well, first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you finished with your notice point? I thought you were moving on to a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will clearly specify when I move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are still on the notice point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Here what's happens then. Because the Prosecution had withdrawn count 12, which was the grave breach count, in March, Judge Mumba, as the Presiding Judge, had ordered the Prosecution prior to trial to file an amended indictment which would redact count 12. So it was purely an effort to clean up the indictment so that this count, which was no longer being alleged, wouldn't appear in the indictment anymore. And what happened was -- now, this is for Judge Shahabuddeen, to answer your question that you posed earlier. This is the indictment. And it says: "Shortly after the events described in 21 and 22." When they amended the indictment, which was only supposed to withdraw this count, in the amendment somebody redacted this. So that's where that disappeared. That was not by order of the Trial Chamber. That was not by motion of the Prosecution. It just disappeared in the amended indictment. Now, again, so what happens? To understand what happened, you have to understand that after the indictment was filed, and after that first witness statement taken by Brenda Hollis was taken, the indictment was then filed, and then the Prosecutor comes into the possession of three additional statements of Witness A. Two are from 1993, one is from 1997. From our perspective, those statements were materially different than her 1995 statement, so we intended to -- again, as we prepared our defence, we intended to impeach Witness A's credibility using those three additional statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I believe what my colleague Judge Robinson had in mind was this: that you have six grounds of appeal and you're still on ground 1, so we're a little preoccupied in mind as to how you propose to reach the other grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Several of the counts I can probably do in about 20 minutes to half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Fine, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will tell the Appeals Chamber, the three that I intend to spend most of my time are on notice, on Witness D's testimony and its conflict and the Trial Chamber's obligation under the European Convention, and sentencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe it would be helpful if you would just summarise the essence of the notice point. I'm interested in what you did at the trial to deal with the lack of notice that you said you had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Here's what happened. Again, we came to trial and had prepared for trial again, as I had indicated. So Witness D comes to trial -- or Witness A, I'm sorry, Witness A comes to trial and testifies now that instead of all of these rapes and sexual assaults by Accused B had happened in the large room prior to trial, she testifies, "I showed up and then Anto Furundzija arrived, and then Anto Furundzija started to interrogate me and he conducted this interrogation, and then Accused B raped me," et cetera, and changed the theory of the case. So now it wasn't that Furundzija was sort of there in the middle at some point, but he was there at the beginning and they were -- Accused B and Furundzija were working together throughout this whole process. Well, my colleague at the trial and I immediately objected, and that is in the record. We objected. Judge Mumba said, "Let Witness A finish her testimony, and then we'll hear your objection." We objected, and I have it here in my notes; I was going to address that. In arguing this motion, I made clear to the Trial Chamber the following two critical points: (A), we were relying on the indictment, so that whole direct and substantial assistance argument which I described was that April 6 motion was contingent upon the allegation that all of this happened before Furundzija's arrival, so we were now prejudiced at trial if they were going to change their theory of the case. The second critical point I made is that because there were no allegations that Furundzija was present in the large room during all of these events, I made no effort to go to Bosnia to find witnesses. She indicated 40 soldiers were there. There was no need, as his Defence counsel, to go find witnesses to explain that he wasn't there. Okay, I'll wrap this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you seek an adjournment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I sought to strike her testimony, and it was granted. That's the point here. I said, "Strike her testimony with respect to everything she said in the large room and only accept it with respect of paragraphs 25 and 26," and they granted my motion. So now we're at trial. We won. We were right. When you, as the Appeal Chamber, retire now, consider the fact that this whole argument that I've laid out for you, the Trial Chamber entered an order on the 12th of June and the 15th of June, saying as follows: "To allow the Prosecution to introduce Witness A's inconsistent testimony now would be a fundamental violation of the accused's right to a fair trial. We hereby will not consider her testimony with respect to anything other than the allegations in 25 and 26," which is that Furundzija arrived -- in 25, I'm sorry, it was that he questioned her and then D made an oral threat and rubbed the knife, and then the pantry. So now we're at trial. We argued to the Trial Chamber that we were being prejudiced, and they granted our motion. So we proceed not going back to find anything about the large room, because why would I do that when I just won the motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, we should be suspending now. But perhaps you could answer, very briefly, one question. You moved to strike the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did the submissions which you made in support of the motion to strike the evidence include any reference to the deletion of those words to which I have referred in paragraph 25 of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: They did not, but there was no need to, because we had relied on -- we had all the pre-trial pleadings, et cetera, and there was no motion from them to amend. It was just, "Clean it up." And what happened was we won the motion to strike her testimony, so we had no reason to rely. I hope that answers Judge Robinson's question also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge Robinson is content. Then we will suspend now for 15 minutes and resume at 20 past the hour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you have the floor, as well as our apologies for being a few minutes behind hand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No problem. Thank you, Your Honour. To try to summarise this issue, we again made our arguments at the trial level, we preserved the record. What's of most importance is we won the motion, so that when I said in my introduction that we were misled, actively misled, the misleading part was that in granting our motion, the Trial Chamber, in effect, told the Defence that, "No, you don't need to call any witnesses about whether Mr. Furundzija was present in the large room, since that is not being charged against you," and so we didn't in our case in chief. The effect -- what happened at judgement, however, shows that the Trial Chamber committed error in not following its own June 12 and June 15 orders. So in addition to all the notice issues that we had talked about, and specifically now an issue was raised with respect to an amended indictment and the portion being stricken, once on the 12th of June the Trial Chamber granted our motion and told us our argument is right and that Mr. Furundzija's right to a fair trial is threatened if we don't take action to strike her testimony, then their failure to do so in the judgement amounts to reversible error. I intend to spend about another five minutes on this issue, Your Honours, and then I'll move on. This issue can be summarised by the following chart, which appears also in our appellate brief. It's identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I would like to follow you. Do I collect that what you are saying is this: that as a result of your successful motion on inadmissibility and the decision of the Trial Chamber to exclude certain evidence, you were left with paragraphs 25 and 26 of the amended indictment. Those were the paragraphs on which you relied for notice as to what were the allegations you had to meet. And your case is that the testimony or the findings of the Trial Chamber diverged from those paragraphs. Perhaps I do not understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly what I am saying. And I will demonstrate how. I think I see sort of where you are leaning with that, so I am going to try to address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No, Mr. Misetic, I am not leaning at all. I am just trying to grasp your submissions at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Better said. There is an issue that's been raised in my head that I would like to address, to clear up any ambiguity. I am exactly saying that the Trial Chamber did not adhere to its own order to apply paragraph 25 and 26. And in one sentence I will say, if paragraph 25 and 26 could be read to allow testimony that Anto Furundzija was there from the beginning and was present in the large rooms during rape and sexual assault, then there would be no reason for the Trial Chamber to have struck the testimony in the first place. So our interpretation, as I took you through it of what happened in the Pre-Trial stage, is unquestionably the interpretation that the Trial Chamber agreed with in granting our motion and in finding that to allow the testimony would be a fundamental breach of their right to a fair trial. This is, again -- in brief, you have this chart in your books. This is what was charged before trial, and the box indicates where Furundzija is alleged to have appeared. All of these events happened before, as I've repeated numerously throughout this argument. And then he is charged with asking her questions in the large room. At the end of all of this, a verbal threat, coupled with the rubbing of a knife, and the issue for the Trial Chamber was, if this is torture. Then he leaves the big room with Witness A, takes her to the pantry, and then the interrogations and the sexual assaults in front of Witness D. And this is what -- again, the Trial Chamber granted our motion at trial that this is the correct interpretation of what the charges are. For the first time, in the judgement, we learn that this is what the Trial Chamber was going to do. She arrives, then Furundzija arrives and begins to interrogate her. So you can see from the juxtaposition here the difference in charges and in substance. And then I am not going to take up my time with going through this, since you have copies in your book. But it's clear that it's the same thing that I've shown throughout my morning argument. The judgement winds up, putting him at the beginning, and then accused B arriving, and from these factual conclusions come several conclusions in the judgement about concerted action, about dividing the process of interrogation, et cetera, et cetera. And then simultaneously reject one of the principal arguments of the Defence at trial, which was the whole direct and substantial assistance, and whether there can be directive and substantial assistance if the perpetrator actually committed all of these crimes on multiple occasions prior to the alleged aider and abettor's appearance on the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying the Trial Chamber relied for its judgement on the evidence in relations to counts 9, 10 and 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. And in addition -- there is no question that they did, and there is no question that they wound up putting him there at the beginning, and that these findings are inconsistent with the way the indictment is set out. The other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The judgement is not explicable, you are saying? You don't rely on the evidence in the counts 9, 10, and 11? Are you saying the judgement is not explicable in absence of a reliance on evidence from counts 9, 10, and 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. As I tried to articulate earlier, there is no -- there is no explanation for why -- how the Trial Chamber could have granted the motion and said it was only going to consider evidence consistent with 25 and 26. There is no explanation for why they granted our motion in the first place, if -- two things: One, they were going to accept her testimony at trial, which was contrary to the indictment that Furundzija was there at the beginning. And two, after having said that they wouldn't consider evidence of the accused's presence or being present during rape and sexual assault in the large room, they then introduced that evidence, but make it appear as though Furundzija was there first and then left, knowing that this woman was going to be raped by Accused B upon his exit from the large room. And what we are saying is that was never alleged in the indictment, and is in fact contrary to not only the indictment, but all of the pre-trial pleadings and finally the Trial Chamber's own order of the 12th of June. And again, all I can say, if this argument were wrong, then the June 12th order is entirely inexplicable, because they accepted our argument and found that all of this was happening and was threatening our right to a fair trial. And I then remind you again, had they not granted the order, had they said, "Mr Misetic, you are wrong; the amended indictment allows the Prosecutor to introduce this evidence and rely on it for conviction, by putting your client there earlier," then I would have had the opportunity to seek a recess on the basis of that order, and then travel back to Bosnia and try to find witnesses about what happened. But now we were -- we were caught completely unprepared, because not only did they grant the motion and then not rely on it, but we also were then misled about whether we had to put a case on in chief about the large room. So in both --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Forgetting the motion. The evidence is relevant. Forgetting the motion, it would seem to me that the evidence in counts 9, 10 and 11 is relevant evidence to what took place in counts 12, 13 and 14. But you are saying that in the way that the trial was conducted, you made a motion, the motion was granted, and as a result of that, you didn't line up your Defence in a particular way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I need to correct you on one point and agree with you on another. First, I wanted the evidence -- I agreed with you that the evidence in counts 9, 10 and 11 is relevant, and I wanted it introduced at trial through Witness A into evidence in the way it appears in counts 9, 10 and 11. What I am saying is the judgement is inconsistent with counts 9, 10 and 11. So they didn't prove 9, 10 and 11. They proved something else. They allege now that Furundzija was there at the beginning of count 9, which isn't the way the indictment is set out. So the defendant is the one that wants to confirm your conclusion that 9, 10 and 11 are relevant. They are relevant because his Defence was predicated, at least in part, on count 9, 10 and 11; namely, this woman was raped and sexually assaulted numerous times before he allegedly appeared. And that's what 9, 10 and 11 say. So I agree with you. And then the other portion that I agree with you on is: And then once they granted our motion -- because if you look at the transcripts, there is a point in my argument on this motion, when I specifically told the Court: What I want to know from the Court is are we facing allegations that Anto Furundzija was there at the beginning? If we are, we need to know that now so that we can put on a case in chief. So we have double prejudice. A, we want 9, 10 and 11 to be into evidence as pled; and B, if they weren't going to do that, if they said the Defence motion, which is now on appeal substantively the same, is wrong, then at least we would have had the opportunity to, at trial, try to introduce evidence. But what happened was the motion was granted, the Defence proceeds on 25 and 26, and then relied on D to knock out the allegations in 26, namely, D's testimony that D only -- D only testifies that B is the interrogator in the pantry, and never that Furundzija is the interrogator in the pantry. And that was our argument. The only rape and sexual assault he is alleged to have interrogated anyone in, happened in the pantry. And we had a Prosecution witness come to trial and testify, to use language in the Prosecutor's appellate brief, testified inconsistently with Witness A on that issue. We believe contradictory to, but I don't want to argue semantics here on language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just let me understand you. Is it your case as follows: that paragraph 25 of the amended indictment makes no allegation of rape, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Your case is you moved successfully to strike evidence of rape in relation to the large room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. My argument is: Witness A's testimony should only have been admitted for purposes of proving the allegations in paragraph 25. That is to say, it's not just striking the testimony that he was present for rape in the large room; it is that her testimony, in placing him there at the beginning, changes the case. In terms of scienter, in terms of -- I forget the language now -- conspiracy, in terms of concert of action. It's crucial. So, from our perspective, we were agreeable at trial to the language of the order, which was: If the Trial Chamber wanted to use Witness A's testimony to prove that Anto Furundzija was present in the large room and started asking questions, at which point in time Accused B threatened her and rubbed his knife on her body, for those purposes we agree that that was alleged before trial, and we had notice of that allegation. So if the Trial Chamber wanted to use that testimony for that purpose, it was proper. But then we had all the legal issues that I talked about, whether it amounts to torture, et cetera. Any other purpose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have at hand the precise wording of the Trial Chamber's ruling?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have -- just a minute. I have document 274 in the record. And the ruling was as follows: "It will only consider as relevant Witness A's evidence insofar as it relates to paragraphs 25 and 26, as pleaded in the amended indictment against the accused." Then the Prosecution filed a motion to clarify, and then they go on and say: "The Trial Chamber ruled inadmissible --" I'm sorry, this is document 281 at pages 1471 and 72. "The Trial Chamber rules inadmissible all evidence relating to rape and sexual assault perpetrated on --" I think it says "Victim A", but it should say "Witness A by the individual identified as Accused B in the presence of the accused in the large room," and then further ordered that it would admit all evidence relating to the allegations detailed in paragraph 26 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, do I understand you correctly to be submitting that contrary to that ruling, the Trial Chamber proceeded to find and to rely on the presence of the accused while an act of rape was being committed in the large room?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. My argument is based on that it will only consider as relevant Witness A's evidence insofar as it relates to paragraph 25 and 26 as pleaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's converse from what the Presiding Judge just said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Converse?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that the converse to what the Presiding Judge just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was afraid that your reading of that would be too limited, in that because they gave that order, then in the judgement what winds up happening is they say, "Yes, we gave the order, so we won't consider that he was physically present while these rapes were taking place, but we will consider that he left her there to be raped by Accused B," which for our purposes, Your Honours, is not much of a substantive difference if he's present or leaves her to be present in the course of this entire judgement and putting him there at the beginning. The fact is that this is, in fact, inconsistent with the amended indictment as pleaded in 25 and 26. Again, had they gone to judgement and then built a judgement around the following facts, and that is all of this happened to Witness A prior to Furundzija arriving, he arrives, and now we're going to address what happened to her in terms of the rubbing of the knife during questioning, address all the legal issues with respect to that, and then go into the pantry and determine what exactly happened in the pantry. Whether Witness A is right or Witness D is right in terms of whether Furundzija was ever involved in any interrogation in the pantry, et cetera, that, from our perspective, was what the Trial Chamber was supposed to be doing in arriving at a judgement. Instead, where we were misled and where we have suffered serious prejudice is that they put him at the beginning and then alleged that this was all, in effect, a conspiracy and a concert of action, when it's charged as Accused B is this rapist and torturer from here through August 1, which is ten weeks later, and Furundzija is alleged to have arrived somewhere in the middle of all this and did this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Does paragraph 25 of the indictment itself, of which you had notice, specify or stipulate any particular sequence of events?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does, Your Honour. Not only does the indictment do so --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's a couple of things to keep in mind. First -- yes, that's it. You need to keep three things in mind on that question. (A), if you read paragraph 25, it says, again, "shortly after the events described in paragraphs 21 and 22."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I should qualify my question by saying that I meant to ask it in relation to this finding or allegation of rape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, can you rephrase?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Does paragraph 25 stipulate any particular sequence in respect of any suggestion of rape?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. The rapes occur in paragraph 24, so there is no -- I mean it says, specifically, that he penetrated Witness A's mouth -- Accused B penetrated Witness A's mouth, vagina and anus with his penis; rape. Twenty-five then says "after the events described in 23 and 24." And then keep in mind two additional things. Keep in mind that in order to avoid any ambiguity, we filed our pre-trial motions to specify, which they were ordered to do, and then that takes us to the two documents I talked about earlier, May 1 and May 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Where are the words "after the events?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right here. "The Prosecutor may want to apply --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No. In paragraph 25 of the indictment, are there any words which read "after the events described in paragraph 24"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think you may be looking at the amended indictment instead of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I am, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I thought you asked me about the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, the amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that's where I'm saying several things. There is no legal basis that that should have been redacted, and it is an oversight, because you can look at the transcripts and it's clear that by sua sponte, the Bench ordered the Prosecution to remove count 12. There was never any discussion about removal of "after this". In the amended indictment also, they redact everything other than 13 and 14. To us, there was no critical issue there, because for our purposes, it is a redacted indictment so as to clean it up. But there was no substantive difference. I would again say that in their pre-trial pleadings, they allege that things happened beforehand. On appeal, in their response brief, they have conceded that the pre-trial brief does allege that certain events took place prior to Mr. Furundzija's alleged arrival. And then finally my argument is worst-case scenario, if you were to say that, "Well, perhaps the fact that this doesn't appear in the amended indictment puts you on notice," in addition to my argument that there was never an amended indictment in the legal sense of Rule 50 because there was never any such motion, that's point 1. And point 2, once the Trial Chamber affirmed our interpretation at trial, they granted our motion telling us we were right, then we had a right to rely on that order. Okay. Sort of scattered here, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have a right to full defence, which was adversely affected?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, because, as I'm saying, the only thing we wanted was fairness. If the Trial Chamber was going to be of the opinion that, "You can admit Witness A's testimony, the amended indictment, you know, somehow now doesn't have this language," et cetera, fine, because we had not yet put on our case in chief on that point. And I specifically said, "If you're going to rule that way, I need to know. I need a recess, I need to go to Bosnia and now start finding witnesses about what happened in room 1, since Witness A said at trial that this happened in front of approximately 40 people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's why I don't see it so much as a notice point, because if an indictment is drafted in a particular way and at the trial evidence is adduced as to facts that were not in the indictment, I mean to my mind that doesn't invalidate the indictment. I think it would entitle you to ask for an adjournment so that you can prepare and meet the new allegations of facts. But I think your real point is that on the basis of the ruling that was given, you had a proper expectation that the case could be managed in a particular way, and therefore, as you said, you did not seek to call any evidence in relation to the evidence arising out of counts 9 to 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would respectfully disagree with you with respect to the earlier portion about whether we're entitled to rely on the indictment at trial, but I would -- and also say that this argument that I'm espousing now was agreed to by the Trial Chamber. But you're absolutely right with respect to the fact that, you know, regardless ultimately of that issue, there is the other issue of once they ruled in our favour, we were entitled to rely on that. One way or the other, we raised this issue, and if they were going to rely on it at judgement, then we should have been told that then, our motion should have been denied, or they should have ordered a recess, or something to that effect. But to grant the motion and then leave us in a position of not going to find witnesses after we specifically, on the record, told them that that is what we needed to do if that was going to be the Trial Chamber's ruling, then we would have been prejudiced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, what parts of the judgement do you rely on as demonstrating that the Trial Chamber walked back, as it were, on their decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The first exhibit I gave you, which is A1, do you still have that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The first finding that Furundzija was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear. Could the counsel speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to try to keep pivoting my head. The first finding that Furundzija was in the room before Accused B appeared is one such contrary finding. That he commenced an interrogation without Accused B is another factual finding. I'm assuming -- I'm sorry, you're asking me about factual findings as opposed to legal conclusions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Factual findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The finding in paragraph A that Accused B then arrived is contrary to the order of June 12. That Furundzija asked a question and then Accused B grabbed Witness A by the hair, put a knife to her throat, and forced her to undress, that is completely contrary. And if you read 23 and 24, this event is alleged to have happened in counts 9 through 11, not 12 through 14. But now, because they've put them there at the beginning, it's during questioning by Furundzija the knife to the throat was placed. Well, that's inconsistent and that's prejudicial to us, because again -- and all along, keep in mind that when you read these findings, there's an ultimate conclusion that the Prosecution proved concert of action. Well, if all of these things are wrong, Furundzija continued to interrogate Witness A while she was forced to remain naked in front of 40 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Don't let me take you away from the schedule you had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Judge, I'm more than happy, and actually I like it better when you ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I appreciate your answers. We'll hear the Prosecution later on and consider what they have to say in response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'm going to, I think, if the Trial Chamber has no other -- I'm sorry, the Appellate Chamber has no other questions on the issue of notice and the June 12th order, then I will move on to issue 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. [Inaudible]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me be precise on which issue this is. This is issue 1B and 1C. I am going to argue them together. And this is, again, when I talked earlier in the morning about what is the most pivotal, factual finding in the case, and that is that Mr. Furundzija conducted an interrogation of Witness A while she was being raped and sexually assaulted. There is -- I don't think there is any dispute among the parties or the Trial Chamber that there is a key witness whom everybody agrees was present throughout, and that is Witness D. So Witness D was in the pantry from the beginning of what happened in the pantry, at least through where Mr. Furundzija is alleged to have left the scene. Now, Witness A's testimony was that -- at trial, was that Mr. Furundzija was present inside the room; that accused B's torture, i.e. his beatings and his rape and sexual assault, was parallel to Mr. Furundzija's questioning. In the judgement, based on that testimony, the Trial Chamber concluded that Witness A was raped and sexually assaulted in the course of an interrogation by the accused, and therefore the accused is a co-perpetrator by virtue of his interrogation of her as an integral part of that torture. The problem, from our perspective, is that the judgement is completely silent about the testimony of one of the Prosecution's witnesses, and that is Witness D. In the Prosecution's brief at paragraph 3.73, they concede that the evidence is not dispositive of whether the appellant was engaged in asking questions in the pantry. The appellant's position on appeal, Your Honour, is that the evidence must be dispositive, that is, conclusive on appeal, as to that critical issue. What did Witness D say? If you read his testimony, whereas Witness A puts Furundzija in the room from the beginning, questioning her -- she says questioning Witness D, while he is being beaten by Accused B, then questioning her while she is being raped and sexually assaulted by Accused B. Witness D's version of events at trial was, and he specifically testified, that Accused B started to interrogate him -- it was Accused B who was the interrogator -- then started to beat him; that Accused B started then to interrogate Witness A. After starting his interrogation of Witness A, Accused B is alleged to have raped Witness A in Witness D's presence. The Prosecution put to Witness D, "Where was Mr. Furundzija at this time?" And Witness D says, "He was outside the room." Now, without going into the issue of whether he was actually outside the room or not, I would first submit that there is a substantive difference between their two testimonies: Namely, is Anto Furundzija the interrogator in the pantry of both Witness D and Witness A, as Witness A testifies? Or is Witness D correct, that Anto Furundzija is not in the room, that Accused B is the interrogator, that Accused B -- I'm sorry -- that Accused B is the interrogator of both D and A, and that he is the physical assaulter of D and the rapist of Witness A? This was, by our count, Your Honours, put to the Trial Chamber, according to our count in the record, more than 50 times, and yet the judgement makes no effort to resolve that conflicting testimony or, to take us back to my standard of review, to explain how it applied the standard of beyond a reasonable doubt to those two testimonies. We were entitled, first of all, to an acquittal on the basis of this testimony and, secondly, to an explanation in the judgement as to how this standard of review was applied. I would argue that there is certainly a fair and rational inference in the evidence that Anto Furundzija did not interrogate anyone in the pantry. Some of these conclusions of the Trial Chamber are indeed inexplicable. Here is one conclusion that I wish to call your attention to: "The Trial Chamber finds beyond a reasonable doubt that Witness D was interrogated by the accused in the pantry." And yet there is no effort, for example, to explain why the Trial Chamber would accept Witness A's version of that and not Witness D's, who does not testify to any interrogation by Anto Furundzija of him in the pantry. It's inexplicable to me how the Trial Chamber could have accepted Witness A's version of what happened to Witness D, and not Witness D's version of what happened to Witness D. And the problem is compounded by the fact that there is no effort made in the judgement to explain any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And your case was that Mr. Furundzija --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is the precise point that I put to the Trial Chamber on at least 50 occasions. So there can be no argument that this was a side argument, a fringe argument that I had made that perhaps the Trial Chamber overlooked. Fifty times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You put it "50 times," but was there some evidence on which the Trial Chamber could have concluded as it did?
