Is your case then this: that the Trial Chamber did not motivate its finding, did not give any reasons for selecting a particular piece of evidence as that on which it had found its conclusion? And/or is your submission this: that the Trial Chamber's finding on that point was not reasonable?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Neither. My submission is not that there was no basis for the finding, but there was no basis for not finding that he wasn't in the pantry. Again, the very nature of the way you pose the question is something that I -- I don't know how to phrase it. It is not an issue of whether the Trial Chamber could reasonably have found something in the evidence to make that conclusion. The burden of proof is beyond a reasonable doubt, so what the issue is, is there a basis in the evidence to conclude that he is not guilty. That's the basis that they should be looking for. And if there is a reasonable basis in the evidence that he is not guilty, that is what "beyond a reasonable doubt" means. And if there is a fair or rational basis, they are required by law to accept it. And from our position, it is unquestionably true that when a Prosecution witness, whom the Prosecution -- whose credibility and whose veracity the Prosecution vouches for, both implicitly and literally at closing argument, and that witness says, "Anto Furundzija was outside the room," when that witness says, "It was Accused B who was the interrogator and rapist in the room," then that, by definition, is a fair -- there is a fair hypothesis that he wasn't in the room and he wasn't interrogating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not if there was other evidence that he was in the room. Then it would be a matter for the Trial Chamber, as the trier of fact, to determine what evidence it would accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The question is -- in this particular situation, for the Trial Chamber to reject a witness who is not impeached, who is a Prosecution witness, and who the Trial Chamber has no reason to or gives no reason to say is not a credible witness, then assuming that that is true, in that situation the evidence has to be overwhelming. In other words, there is a videotape that shows that Witness D is wrong and Witness A is right, but where you have conflicting eyewitness testimony, conflicting eyewitness testimony, and you have -- I mean, it's not even my witness; it's the Prosecution's witness. There is clearly a fair inference of innocence there. I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that the mere fact that there is conflicting testimony must lead to the -- must give rise to a reasonable doubt. The mere fact that there is conflict in the evidence must give rise to reasonable doubt. Is that your proposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The fact that in this case we had a witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Isn't that classically the function of a Trial Chamber, how to assess conflicting evidence, on the basis of demeanour of witnesses, to determine who is reliable, who is credible? Isn't that a classical function of a Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One problem is that we don't know how they resolved that issue. So all we are left to do here is speculate as to what the Trial Chamber's ultimate conclusion was, whether they even considered Witness D's testimony. The fact of the matter is, the Prosecution put that evidence in. We relied on it. If -- assuming arguendo, that that is the correct position, if the Trial Chamber had a reasonable -- had a basis to conclude that Witness D's testimony was less credible and less reliable than Witness A's testimony, then the other argument is we have a right to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, my mind travels along similar lines to those of my colleague, Judge Robinson. Is it your case, and it is your case which I am trying to grasp, this: In a case involving a multitude of evidential discrepancies, it is the function of the Trial Chamber to resolve those discrepancies and to announce its finding, its conclusions of fact. Is it your case that when it does so, it has to embark on an analysis of each discrepancy so as to present a reasoned conclusion as to why it has resolved a particular discrepancy in a particular way?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would amend that somewhat and base my formulation on the European Court of Human Rights, and say that it does not need to address every inconsistency, but it certainly needs to address any determinative -- a reasonable hypothesis or a reasonable submission on a determinative issue. So I cited the Hiro Balani case from the European Court of Human Rights. If the discrepancy is on a determinative issue, then yes, the Trial Chamber has an obligation to explain why it accepted one version of events over another. It does not need to explain why it chose the 16th of May as the day of the incident instead of the 17th of May, for example. But on an issue of where the entire case hinges on whether this man conducted an interrogation of a woman while she is being raped, and we have a Prosecution witness who comes in the Court and says: "He was not in the room, he was not interrogating anyone; it was Accused B who did all of this," then, yes, we are entitled to at least an explanation. Furthermore, I think as a matter of law there is reasonable doubt. And it would take me another hour to go through -- I won't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: On that point, may I suggest to you that we be all mindful of the clock at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I will cut short --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Court is agreeable to giving you as much time as you need, provided you conclude before the luncheon break. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, Your Honours. Another issue that I wish to raise -- this is two minutes -- is the judgement makes several findings with respect to Witness D. And I wish the Appellate Chamber to do a review of these findings. In paragraph 267, in determining whether the elements of torture have been met, the Trial Chamber considers Witness D's suffering, et cetera, in concluding that Mr. Furundzija's guilty of torture. In paragraph 121, the Trial Chamber finds that both Witness A and Witness D were subjected to severe physical and mental suffering and also were particularly humiliated. Then finally, in paragraph 281, we have evidence that the Trial Chamber found that Witness D was tortured, and that is that in determining aggravating factors, the Trial Chamber found that Mr. Furundzija's function was to interrogate Witness A in the large room, and in the pantry, where he also interrogated Witness D, while both were being tortured by Accused B. So, clearly, in that sentence it appears that the Trial Chamber found that Witness D was tortured, and considered that evidence in sentencing. And the problem, from the Defence's perspective, is that we can find no support, and it -- I don't submit it's because there isn't any, but only because we have made diligent efforts to find authority for the proposition that when one soldier in an army assaults another soldier in his own army, that he has committed an international war crime. And indeed Rule 2 specifically says -- defines a victim as a person against whom a crime over which the Tribunal has jurisdiction has been committed. In this case, Mr. Furundzija was convicted of torturing a man, an active combatant in his own army. And the issue that I put to the Appellate Chamber for review is whether the Trial Chamber had jurisdiction to consider that. And the key issue, then, is whether the physical assault of one soldier of another in his own army is -- could be an international war crime. And I would ask you to consider that Witness D was considered in both the consideration of guilt and in -- as an aggravating factor in sentencing. And so if, indeed, the Trial Chamber did not have jurisdiction, then that is yet another issue to reverse. Briefly, on the European Convention. I wanted to point out, again reiterate our position that under the European Convention and the jurisprudence of the European Court, the Trial Chamber was under an obligation to address well-founded submissions on determinative issues. And we believe that Witness D's contrary testimony was indeed clearly a well-founded submission on a determinative issue, and for that reason they should have addressed the issue. We also wish to point out to the Trial Chamber that we are opposed, and consider it to be a violation of Mr. Furundzija's rights, if the Appellate Chamber were to now go back and try to determine what the Trial Chamber's reasoning was, or how the Trial Chamber resolved that conflicting testimony. And the basis of that objection is that we believe that is a violation of Article 21 (4)(b), in terms of being able to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation, in this case, of his appeal. He's entitled to know now, so that he can appeal how the Trial Chamber applied the standard of beyond a reasonable doubt to the evidence between A and D. If, for the first time, he finds out the reason for why -- I hesitate to even say A's was accepted, because that is just an assumption and not -- there are other hypotheses for why D's evidence wasn't considered, but that A's testimony was selected as truthful. If he finds that out for the first time in the appellate judgement, then he has no place to appeal that the standard of beyond a reasonable doubt, as applied to the explanation in this case now by the Appellate Chamber, that that standard was misapplied. And so we argue that you must take the record and the judgement for what it is, and that is that we have an issue that was unaddressed, and if you find that the testimony of Witness D was a well-founded submission, and a fair and rational hypothesis could be made from that testimony, that he in fact did not interrogate anyone in the pantry, then you must reverse the judgement. You must reverse the judgement. The next issue is whether Anto Furundzija was denied his right to attain the evidence and examination of relevant witnesses on his behalf. To understand what happened at trial would take much more time than I have. After the trial went to deliberation by the Trial Chamber in June of '98, we received notice from the Office of the Prosecutor as to certain documents that were not produced. We filed a motion to strike Witness A's testimony in its entirety for the failure to comply with Rule 68. The Trial Chamber denied the motion to strike and reopened the proceedings for the limited purpose of examining medical, psychological -- for the limited purpose of dealing only with medical, psychological, or psychiatric treatment of Witness A. The Defence proposed several witnesses -- first, the Defence disagreed with the proposition that a Trial Chamber or -- the trier of fact, having retired to deliberate on the evidence, can go back and reopen the trial on the basis of a finding that the Prosecution had committed misconduct. Nevertheless -- and we filed an appeal on that basis, and that was rejected. The Defence then prepared for the reopening and proposed two witnesses. One is the person whom we have now labelled as Witness F, and the other was an individual named Enes Surkovic. Witness F, for background purposes, was a Croat soldier in the HVO who, towards the end of Witness A's ordeal, had taken -- he and his wife had taken in Witness A sometime in August of '93, and had hid her from Accused B and from others until she could be exchanged and transferred over to her family in a different part of Bosnia. We had no reason to call this witness, other than now at issue was going to be what was her psychological, psychiatric, medical, mental, et cetera, states, which was what the Trial Chamber had ordered that it wanted to hear evidence on. So we made a search for this person and found him, and he provided evidence to us which we thought was clearly relevant. For the reopening of the trial, he discussed Witness A's medical, psychological and psychiatric symptoms that he had encountered, including that she was suicidal, that she was having medical difficulties, et cetera, all things that I think most people would find to be a logical consequence of the events that had transpired. He was also the first person who took her for medical treatment. In addition to that, he offered exculpatory evidence for Mr. Furundzija, and that is that he had known Mr. Furundzija when both were members of the Bosnian army, that is, the army of BiH in the Central Bosnia region. He had found Mr. Furundzija -- well, in any event, actually he had found him to be someone who would not be participating in this. And he told us that he specifically asked her about him because the two of them were friends and that she told him that, "Oh, when Furundzija was around, no one would touch me." And I can't recall, off the top of my head, what the other statement was, but it was exculpatory. So we put his name down -- I'm sorry, we sought the Trial Chamber's assistance in getting that testimony in, and the Trial Chamber denied, as being irrelevant, that testimony. We object here, on appeal, to the denial of the right to call him. He is a fact witness as to her medical -- he is the first fact witness, in that he had firsthand knowledge while she was still technically in HVO territory, and, second, he had exculpatory evidence which was clearly relevant to his guilt or innocence and to her credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At what stage did you seek to adduce this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It was in July of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. In what stage of the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Within two weeks of when the Trial Chamber ordered the reopening of the case, so relatively early. That was denied. That later came to be relevant, because at trial, the first witness we recalled was Dr. Mujezinovic, and Dr. Mujezinovic's testimony was relevant because he testified that in the fall of '93, he had encountered her, that he found her to be in serious difficulty in terms of psychological, psychiatric, et cetera, that he had referred her for medical help, that she couldn't string two sentences together, et cetera. The same day, Witness A took the stand and completely denied just about everything that Dr. Mujezinovic had testified to as to what her state was and, indeed, indicated that she had, other than on one occasion in August of '93, had not even received any medical assistance since that time. So Witness F's testimony was clearly relevant, because it would have confirmed Dr. Mujezinovic's version of the events that transpired and what her mental, psychological and psychiatric state was from August of '93 through the fall and through what turned out to be 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I have the reopening order made by the Trial Chamber before me, and am I right that it speaks not only of further evidence relating to medical, psychological and psychiatric matters generally but that it is confined rather more narrowly to treatment or counselling? It says: "Cross-examination to be strictly --" "Defence may recall any Prosecution witness for cross-examination strictly on any medical, psychological, or psychiatric treatment or counselling," and those words are repeated in items 2 and B1. Now, did this witness to whom you have referred, did he participate in giving any treatment or counselling?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was the first person who provided her with treatment. He physically didn't. He took her to someone who did. And, second, he had information about pills that she was taking, et cetera. And then, third, with respect to the treatment, ultimately his testimony is relevant because in the judgement the Trial Chamber, in our view, makes a rather stretched interpretation such that it concludes that it was -- that Witness A could have gone through treatment without knowing that she was going through treatment. And so in terms of that ultimate conclusion, then, this testimony is relevant in the sense that it assists the trier of fact in determining whether that interpretation is possible, whether someone who was in the state as described by Witness F, as described by Dr. Mujezinovic, and as we think would have been described by the next witness that I'm going to talk about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Was the witness a medically trained or qualified person?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But the fact of the matter is there aren't many medically trained people that we could have found on that issue, particularly if you're going to use a term like "qualified." We had to take the evidence as it was, and this was an eyewitness. The same argument, in essence, applies to the next witness, and that is Enes Surkovic. He, by Witness A's own admission, saw her in the late fall of 1993. He is also an eyewitness as to what had transpired. We believe he is a hostile witness to the Defence, and therefore we did not have an opportunity to interview him, other than to get him to trial and to have him testify by subpoena, if necessary, as to what he knew and what he saw. The other critical area which we didn't know at the time, which turned out to be that way in the judgement, is that the first witness statement that we have from Witness A is, from our view, extremely inconsistent throughout but especially with respect to Mr. Furundzija, and in closing argument, we relied heavily on the inconsistencies contained in that '93 statement from her trial testimony and used it to impeach her. She denied at trial that she had ever given a statement, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The other ground of appeal is that then in the judgement, without telling the Defence that they were questioning the foundation of the document, and I would add that this was a Prosecution document, i.e., there was no dispute between the Prosecution and the Defence as to the authenticity of the document, the Court sua sponte declared that it was unreliable, (A), without telling the Defence that it wanted foundation, and, (B), after having had the opportunity to call the person who allegedly took the statement to verify its authenticity. So we were left in a position again of -- one of the principal arguments as to credibility was that witness statement, which it is common practice here at the Tribunal to use witness statements to impeach the reliability and credibility of witnesses. We relied on one such statement to cross-examine. There appeared to be no foundational issues at trial, since the Prosecution had moved it into evidence, and we had no objection to its foundation or authenticity, and then in the judgement to find that the Trial Chamber deals with all these inconsistencies by saying that, "Witness A says it's not hers and therefore we dismiss the statement," having been given the opportunity to subpoena Mr. Surkovic and to hear from him whether he took that statement or not and whether it was authentic. So we object on that basis as well. You, as the Trial Chamber, have the authority to determine whether the evidence that was used in convicting Mr. Furundzija was reliable. There is a substantive difference between credibility and reliability. Credibility is, for the most part, best determined by the trier of fact, in that it's the trier of fact who sat in the trial, who had the opportunity to observe the witness, who had the opportunity to examine the witness, et cetera. Reliability is something that an Appellate Chamber can do just as effectively as the Trial Chamber, in that it's an issue of applying the law to the facts, and therefore you do not need to have sat in the courtroom to know whether the testimony or whether the evidence was reliable. One of our major arguments at trial, Your Honours, was that Witness A could not be deemed a reliable witness; not a credible witness but a reliable witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: As a result of your submissions, there will be a need for a little redaction. The registrar will show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson, I'm almost positive that I'm right, but I will refrain until the break so we can confirm that. Thank you. One of the things that you will have to do is review Witness A's testimony when you retire on this judgement, and one of the things that we have to emphasise is the lack of reliability here, and that is based on several factors. I think this is a critical point, given Judge Robinson's reference earlier to the fact that a Trial Chamber does not have to -- I'm sorry, that conflicting testimony is, per se, reasonable doubt. Here in this particular case, and this is -- after all, what we have to do here is apply the law to the facts of the particular case, and that is that she is not reliable as a matter of law where -- first and foremost, what we talked about earlier, the conflicting testimony between Witness D and Witness A about events in the pantry. Two, what I had talked about earlier, her completely different version of events with respect to her meeting with Dr. Mujezinovic in the fall of '93. So now we have two witnesses in the trial with whom she has diametrically opposed recollections of events. Three is the conflicting witness statements that I've already referred to here, and that formed much of the closing argument on behalf of the defendant. Four, as a matter of law, when the Trial Chamber has to strike Witness A's testimony, because it is inconsistent with the indictment, in order to preserve the accused's right to a fair trial, and that indictment is based on her own 1995 statement, we contend, Your Honours, that as a matter of law, where the Trial Chamber had to interject itself to protect the defendant's right to a fair trial, that that is substantive proof of the lack of reliability of the witness. Now, when you take this and go back to Witness D's argument and what we had talked about earlier with Judge Robinson, and we say that Witness D, who was in no way impeached by the Defence or the Prosecution, gives one version of events and Witness A gives another, and it's already proven at trial that her testimony had to be stricken by the Trial Chamber because of its lack of -- because of its inconsistency with her own statement and, thus, the indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I think it will help you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It will help you to make an orderly conclusion of your interesting presentation if you were to bear in mind that we are hoping to terminate at ten minutes to the hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am right on time, Your Honour. Thank you. Finally, you should consider her identification of Mr. Furundzija in that '95 statement was substantively different than Mr. Furundzija's actual description. One of the things that you should consider is that in 1995, she described him as 172 centimetres, blonde hair, small features. Instead, he is 183 centimetres, dark hair, with some prominent features.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Stand up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Stand up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the law, there was an inconsistency, and I referred to Tadic here and its discussion of identifications. There was no line-up or, to use the British phrase, no parade to select Mr. Furundzija, and the only ID that she gave was an ID in the dock. Tadic says that in-dock identifications are not to be relied on, and I cite you Judge May's own book on criminal procedure, which says that in-dock identifications should at all costs be avoided, if possible, because of their inherit unreliability. All of these factors you should consider in determining whether or not Witness D's testimony should have been accepted, at least to show that there is a fair or rational inference that he didn't do it, and if that fair or rational inference is to be dismissed, his testimony is to be dismissed as no fair or rational inference, then all of the factors that I've just shown you must somehow resolve and explain why her testimony is so much more convincing than D's that it merits the finding that D's testimony does not even merit a fair or rational inference of innocence. Quickly, we raise several issues about factual findings that were made with respect to Ahmici. We strenuously object to those findings. It is unfair that, for example, they make a finding that he personally participated in expelling Muslims from their homes. Well, Mr. Furundzija is not guilty of that, and we had no clue that that was an issue in the case, that we had to put on evidence that he didn't do any such thing, et cetera. And so for that purpose, if for no other reason, we wish to preserve our objection to those types of findings throughout the record as inappropriate and unnecessary to the facts and issues that were involved in this case. Because I'm running short on time, I would propose if the Court has questions on the motion to disqualify, I would address them. If not, I would move on to sentencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Furundzija, as you know, was sentenced to ten years' imprisonment on the basis of the torture count and eight years' imprisonment on the basis of the aiding and abetting of rape, and it is our position, Your Honours, that this sentence, in light of all the evidence at trial, is much too harsh, is inconsistent with the evidence, and is inconsistent with some of the jurisprudence of the International Tribunal. Now, for purposes of sentencing, as much as I hate to do it, I must presume that you will affirm all of the factual and legal findings of the Trial Chamber in convicting Mr. Furundzija, and so I trust you will understand that if I make any implicit assumption of guilt, it is not because I believe it to be so; it is because I must on this argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We're all legally qualified people, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One element to be considered in sentencing is the weight of the evidence in the case. This sentence clearly was a strong sentence, in the Defence's position, a harsh sentence, and particularly when one considers all of the issues that I have raised here, even if ultimately you somehow could come to the conclusion of guilt, where you had the testimony of Witness D, where you had the issue of changing testimony and changing charges, et cetera, in the indictment, that is one element that should be considered at the time of sentencing. I would submit that it is substantively different where you have, for example, 50 witnesses who will come and say somebody did X, Y and Z and committed this crime, and then you sentence him to the maximum penalty because you have zero doubt as to his guilt, and a situation where you have convicted someone, but there are substantive issues that hang over the case and that might suggest an innocent possibility, and that in sentencing, that is something that should be taken into consideration. The second principle that we rely on is the sentencing policy that was followed in the Tadic Trial Chamber the first time around and with respect to sentences imposed for -- and these are the words of the Trial Chamber: "Tadic's acts were incontestably heinous, but his level --" I'm sorry, that was from a different -- that's my next argument. "That he had participated in the beating of a man, involving the use of whips, iron bars, and instruments to inflict great suffering on the victims, as well as terrorising them and near suffocation through a noose." So we have particularly cruel conduct, a cruel form of torture, and the Trial Chamber sentenced Tadic to six years for a violation of the laws and customs of war. Now, there is certainly a discretion and a range that is afforded to the trier of fact, but I would submit that the four-year range here is entirely too much, given that what was given to Tadic was six years' imprisonment. I would also ask the Trial Chamber to consider the recent Tadic Appeals Chamber decisions with respect to sentencing. It is clear that there are issues of great dispute with respect to crimes against humanity versus, quote/unquote, "ordinary war crimes." Some of the distinguished members of the panel have been participants in the resolution of those issues, be it the Erdemovic case or in the Tadic case, and I leave it again for you to decide. We obviously relied on some of those earlier opinions in our appellate brief, but one particular portion of the Appeals Chamber decision in Tadic, which I would ask you to consider here, is that the Appeals Chamber ruled that the Trial Chamber must consider the need for sentences to reflect the relative significance of the accused in the context of the former Yugoslavia. This is a quote, "Tadic's acts were incontestably heinous, but his level in the command structure was relatively low." I would ask you to consider that in terms of your review of this sentence. The accused has never been alleged to be a high-ranking official of any kind and the acts in question are not consistent and systematic, but transpired all within approximately an hour or two on one afternoon in 1993. And so for those reasons, when you compare Mr. Furundzija's ten-year sentence versus Tadic's six, or some of the other sentences that have been handed out, including, I would argue, Mr. Erdemovic's initial ten for the mass participation in the execution of 72 individuals, when there were no mitigating circumstances found at the time of the commission of the offences, I would argue that this sentence is inconsistent with some of these principles and for that reason that the sentence must be reduced. In conclusion, Your Honours, I will try to wrap up quickly and say that in my argument I have hoped to demonstrate to you several key, critical issues that ultimately result in Mr. Furundzija not receiving a fair trial. And as I indicated to you earlier, it is you who are charged with defending those principles and those international covenants and defending the right to a fair trial. And where Mr. Furundzija relied on the indictment, where he made his objections on the record at trial, and made his motion to strike, and that motion was granted, and then he was ultimately misled as to even that order, he cannot be deemed to have received a fair trial. To take it just outside of the legal context and just ask ourselves: Is this fair, just as an impartial observer and a person who is not a Judge or not a lawyer, is this fair? And is it fair that when a Prosecution witness comes in and testifies on behalf of the Prosecution that Mr. Furundzija was not present, interrogating anyone in the pantry, is it fair that that evidence should be apparently summarily dismissed without explanation. Is that fair? And if it isn't fair, and I don't believe it is, then you must act pursuant to your mandate from the Security Council and intervene to protect his right to a fair trial. And I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, we have a minute and a half to go. Perhaps we are not in danger of transgressing the temporal limits which I have set if I ask you a question about ground 4, the disqualification point. I did say I didn't have any questions. May I ask you one question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: In the Court below, did the Defence open any issue as to whether rape was or was not a war crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Misetic, we are indebted to you for your kind assistance this morning. We will now take the adjournment until 2.15, when we will hear counsel for the Prosecution. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.50 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The proceedings resumed. Ready for the Prosecution, Mr. Yapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Before you begin, the Bench is concerned to make sure that the parties understand that we are disposed to be as equitable as possible so far as the allocation of times is concerned, but we understand that you are disposed to finish by a quarter to 4.00. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Excellent. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honour, my purpose in standing up before Your Honours now at this stage is to make a few introductory remarks on the submissions made by my learned friend. My learned friend devoted much of his time, or the time available to him, I should say the major portion, to deal with two issues, the first being the question of the fair trial, and the second on the contradictory nature of the evidence. We are in a position to respond to the submissions made. He restricted himself to those two grounds and made certain submissions on the question of sentence. And also, in the course of his submissions, he made reference to the standard of review that will be applied by Your Honours' Court. With respect, we do not agree with -- I do not agree with my learned friend on the standard of review that he promulgated, which would be applied by Your Honours' Court. We have, in our response submitted, as far as possible, responses, replies to the brief that my learned friend submitted. On the first ground of the fairness of the trial, or the fairness to the accused, Mr. Norman Farrell will make his submissions, and on the question of sentence, it will be Mr. Chris Staker who will make the submissions. On the other grounds that have been placed by my learned friend, if Your Honours have any questions, we'll be happy to answer. I thank Your Honours. Mr. Norman Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The appellant raises grounds of appeal, as you are aware. To a certain extent they are overlapping. They deal with a number of issues. Over and over again, in relation to a number of the different grounds, our submissions are fully set out in our 100-page brief. And what I will be submitting to is the Prosecution's position in relation to the position taken today. I won't be addressing the issues in the brief; at least I'll try not to. In my introduction there is two points that the Prosecution would like to make, or two examples I would like to refer you to, just to clarify the position of the Prosecution. In the appellant's brief, both in his appeal brief and in his reply brief, and specifically in his reply brief, he characterises the Prosecution's position on a number of occasions, and he restates the Prosecution's position in a number of places. I would like to refer to two places where, in the Prosecution's respectful submission, it's clear that he has characterised the Prosecution's submissions incorrectly, or the position of the Prosecution. And, as a result, the Prosecution does not accept the characterisation of its position in the reply brief by the appellant. The first is in relation to -- and I will try to make clear these are not my submissions on these points; these are just to try and clarify what the Prosecution's position is. And it's not as stated in my friend's brief. The first relates to the interrogation by the appellant in the pantry. And as you are fully aware, the issue in that case is whether there is a contradiction between Witness A's testimony that said the appellant interrogated while in the pantry, and Witness D's testimony, which says that the appellant -- his allegation is that the appellant did not interrogate while in the pantry. In his brief on page 35, he refers to the Prosecution's position and says: "The Trial Court's finding that Mr. Furundzija questioned Witness D in the pantry is the linchpin to his conviction. Given the agreement between the parties at the appellate level that, at a minimum, the evidence on this issue is not dispositive, the Appeals Chamber must reverse the Trial Chamber." With respect, and this may have been just a misunderstanding from our brief, but let me make it absolutely clear. The Prosecution's position is not that the evidence on this issue is not dispositive. He takes the position that the evidence on this issue, the evidence of Witness A and Witness D, is not determinative of the issue of whether there was an interrogation. He then derives from that, that the Trial Chamber should have had a reasonable doubt. In other words, the evidence isn't determinative, it isn't conclusive, it isn't clear, about the interrogation in the pantry. He then states that as there's an agreement between the parties at the appellate level that the evidence on this issue, the issue being the interrogation in the pantry, is not dispositive, the Appeals Chamber must reverse. With respect, that's not the position taken in the Prosecution's brief, and you'll see in the brief, at paragraphs 3,67 to 3,73, that what the Prosecution brief says is that Witness D's testimony is not dispositive of the issue of whether the appellant actually interrogated in the pantry. There's other evidence. There's Witness A's testimony that the appellant interrogated in the pantry, and it will be the Prosecution's submission that Witness D, in fact, contrary to my friend's submission, doesn't actually address the issue of whether the appellant asked questions in the pantry. That's not what he testified to. So, with respect, the reference in page 35 is contrary to the position taken, and we don't accept it. That may have just been a misreading in light of his reading, and I'm not alleging any bad faith. The second example I want to refer to which is crucial in our submission is the reply brief at page 14. In the reply brief of the appellant at page 14, it states: "The Prosecution also offers no response to the Defence's argument that the Trial Chamber apparently convicted Mr. Furundzija of war crimes committed against Witness D, an HVO soldier in his own army. The Defence's arguments on this point are thus unrefuted and should be deemed conceded." This is under the heading "Concessions and Admissions by the Prosecution". I would also note it's under a subheading which says: "Reliance on acts committed against Witness D in convicting Mr. Furundzija." The first thing I note is this is a new heading. This heading is not in his appellate brief. The first part of the heading is, but the second part of the heading, which I just read, is not in his appellant brief and is now recharacterised as if it was raised in his appellant's brief. Secondly, the statement says: "The Prosecution offers no response to the Defence's argument that Mr. Furundzija was convicted in relation to Witness D." There is no argument in the appellant's brief on this issue. Let me draw you to the only reference in the appellant's brief that is made on this. In part 5 of the appellant's brief, under his statement of facts, that is, not under his argument, under the statement of facts of the appellant's brief, starting at page 44 under his brief dealing with judgement and sentence, the appellant quotes the judgement of the Trial Chamber. It's a flat quote that goes for a page and a half. At the end of page 45, there's a footnote which is at the end of the judgement and sentence that is quoted. Now, one would assume that that footnote actually should be in reference to the actual quotation, because this is a quotation that he's put in. But if you look at the end, under footnote 3, the appellant says: "Although the judgement is unclear on this point, the Trial Chamber appears to have found Mr. Furundzija guilty of torturing Witness D and to have taken the torture of Witness D into account in sentencing." Then he says: "The Trial Chamber never sets forth any legal basis for convicting Mr. Furundzija of a war crime against an active combatant in his own army." I may be wrong, and I would ask the appellant's counsel to correct me in reply if I am, but this is the only reference that the Prosecution was able to find with respect to this ground of appeal. It is not, with respect, a ground of appeal. There's no allegation of an error, and there's no argument by the Defence on this issue. If you read the footnote, it says: "The judgement is unclear on this point." It appears to me that the appellant is aware of this issue. He decides, in his interpretation, that it's unclear. He does not raise it as an error of law. He does not set it out as a ground of appeal, as required under Rule 111. And he does not seek leave to amend his notice or his appeal brief to raise this as an issue. In respect, it's the contrary. He's addressed his mind to it and he's decided not to raise it, and he puts it in a footnote. In my submission, this issue, if it is an issue, has been waived. It was not raised at the trial level, it was not objected to at the trial level, and it is included in a footnote on page 45 of the brief, and then, in reply, asserts that there's an argument which the Prosecution didn't respond to, and therefore the Prosecution should concede. With respect, I'm not sure what type of practice -- tactic this is, but I would submit that in this Tribunal, that does not comply with the Rules. I stand to be corrected on that. Maybe it is raised somewhere else, but in my respectful submission, it's not. As a result of those two examples which I've just presented to you, the Prosecution's position is clear that we do not accept the allegations or, sorry, the recharacterisation and the statement of the Prosecution's position in the reply brief. That was the essence of that point. I would now like to go on to the substantive issues on the appeal, if I may.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The next issue I would like to raise and make submissions on is the standard of review on appeal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The appellant, in his second and third grounds of appeal, makes essentially allegations or submissions regarding insufficiency of evidence. Specifically, that's the title of the grounds of appeal. He makes certain submissions on the standard that's to be applied by the Appellate Chamber with respect to an assessment of the facts by an Appeal Chamber of a Trial Chamber's ruling. It's the position of the Prosecution that the standard proposed by the appellant is wrong and it's inconsistent with the decision in Tadic. The majority decision in Tadic finds that the findings of fact of a Trial Chamber are to be given great deference and they are to stand, unless no reasonable person could have reached that conclusion on the evidence, and it's only where the evidence, where relied upon, could not reasonably have been accepted by a reasonable person that the Appeals Chamber can intervene. In fact, the Appeals Chamber in Tadic finds that two Judges, both acting reasonably, could come to different conclusions on the evidence. His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen, in a separate opinion, comes to similar conclusions on that issue, stating that different minds, equally competent, may, and often do, arrive at different and equally reasonable results, and Judge Shahabuddeen states that the Appeals Chamber will intervene where it can see that no reasonable person would have taken the view taken by the Trial Chamber. Now, if I can juxtapose the actual language in Tadic to the Defence position, in its brief and as asserted this morning, the Defence states that where a reasonable trier of fact could reasonably conclude, on the basis of all the evidence, that the appellant is not guilty, the Appeals Chamber must intervene. With respect, that's incorrect. You don't sit as an Appeals Chamber to determine whether a reasonable trier of fact might have had a reasonable doubt at trial. That's the standard for the Trial Chamber. As noted in the Tadic decision, the function of the Appellate Chamber is not to retry the issue and determine whether or not a reasonable person would have had a reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You're drawing a distinction, do I understand you, between the standard applicable to the Court below and the standard applicable to the Appeal Court; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You're saying that the Court below has to determine whether there is proof beyond a reasonable doubt, but if there is material which could go either way, the Appeals Chamber will not interfere unless it takes the view that no reasonable person could have come to that conclusion; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. As I think it's clear what the position is, I won't go over any more of the points I make but just reiterate that when the Defence attempts to argue that when a reasonable person could arrive at a different conclusion and therefore this raises a reasonable doubt, this would, in fact, be contrary to the determination in Tadic that two reasonable persons could reasonably arrive at different conclusions. And, in fact, on the standard even applied at the trial level, if there was a two-to-one decision, a majority of two convicting and one finding reasonable doubt, on his standard if a reasonable person could have found a reasonable doubt, and assuming, of course, that a minority Judge who dissents and would acquit is a reasonable person, the two-to-one decision wouldn't hold, and since a reasonable person could have, he should have been acquitted, regardless of the majority decision at trial. So, with respect, it doesn't hold water. The second point regarding the standard relied on is that in his reply brief at page 8, the appellant also mixes up the onus. Not only does he mix up the standard but he mixes up the onus on appeal. On page 8 of his reply brief, the appellant says: "The burden is on the Prosecution to prove that there is no fair or rational basis for concluding that the appellant is not guilty of the crimes charged." He is indicating that the burden is on the Prosecution to prove that no fair rational basis. He reverses the onus and he applies a reasonable doubt standard, both incorrect. What the appellant has done is he's referred to a passage which is in the Tadic appeal brief. And in that passage -- I think it's paragraph 64 or 164. I can get it if it's necessary. In that passage in the Tadic appeal brief, it's the Prosecution appealing against the findings of the Trial Chamber resulting in acquittal. The Prosecution takes the position that the Trial Chamber erred and should have convicted the accused in that circumstance. And the standard the Prosecution submits is that the Prosecution, as the appellant, must demonstrate that no reasonable trier of fact could have acquitted. In other words, the onus is on the Prosecution in that case to show that the only reasonable conclusion on the evidence would have been to convict. The appellant takes that standard, which is the standard of an appellant on appeal, and even though he is the appellant in this case, says, "Well, the onus is on the Prosecution to prove the same standard." With respect, the determination or submission as to the onus submitted by my colleague for the appellant is incorrect as well. That standard in Tadic was the standard applied by the appellant in that case, and that's the same standard that he must apply as the appellant in this case. That's just a short introduction on the standard. If I can move now to the substantive grounds. I would now like to deal with the ground of the sufficiency of the evidence as alleged by the appellant. I note that the appellant spent an extraordinary amount of time explaining to the Appeals Chamber his submissions at trial, which resulted in him getting a remedy which he had requested. The only relevance that the Prosecution conceived is that there might be have been some prejudice, once he got the remedy, because the Trial Chamber relied on the evidence which was supposed to have been excluded or not relied on. I think that's his submission. With respect, the complaint was that there was a problem with the indictment and therefore he was granted a remedy. I can't imagine that he's complaining at this point in time that the remedy he granted was in error. It was the remedy he asked for. Secondly, with respect, it's not a sufficiency of the indictment issue. The indictment is valid. It's clear what the scope of the indictment is. The question before you is whether the Trial Chamber erred in granting the variation -- or responding to the variance at trial. What appears to have happened, quite simply, is that there was certain evidence which was in pre-disclosure documents which related to some conduct which the Defence alleges was not within the scope of paragraph 25 and 26. The Defence alleges that he relied on this sequence of events, which he alleges in the pre-disclosure documents demonstrate that the appellant was not present at the beginning of the interrogation of Witness A and arrived after the fact. And that's what paragraph 24 and 25 relate to. His reliance on -- extensively on counts 9 to 11, in my respectful submission, are somewhat irrelevant. Counts 9, 10, 11 were not before the Trial Chamber. Counts 9, 10, 11 -- he was not charged with counts 9, 10, 11, he was not arraigned at his initial appearance in relation to counts 9, 10, 11, and the fact that he had the indictment was simply because that was the indictment for a broader group of accused in which his charges were taken out. That's evident from the amended indictment, which was filed on June 2nd, 1998, upon which this trial proceeded. The trial did not proceed on the basis that the appellant is submitting to you. It did not proceed on the evidence that he submits was clearly before the Trial Chamber and was the basis of the charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You say that the allegations in the original indictment relating to counts 9, 10 and 11 did not form part of the amended indictment on the basis of which a trial in fact proceeded. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The appellant's reliance on counts 9, 10 and 11 to formulate the strategy upon which he intended to proceed, that was his choice. And, of course, he can rely on the Pre-Trial brief to formulate the strategy upon which he intends to proceed. That's fine. The scope of the indictment is with respect to particular acts that took place during the time that Mr. Furundzija was there conducting an interrogation against Witness A in conjunction with accused B. That's the scope of paragraph 25 and 26. 26 of course -- not broadens it, is a continuation into the pantry. But that's the scope of paragraph 25 and the commencement of the charges against the appellant. If the appellant alleges that he relied on Pre-Trial disclosure documents to formulate his Defence, which is not even part of paragraphs 25 and 26, this sequence that he is relying on. Paragraph 25, 26 do not set out any sequence. They set out conduct that the appellant --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The interpreters are appealing to you again. Could you restrain your natural tendency to speed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'll do my best. My apologies to the interpreters. The -- I'm sorry. My point was that if the appellant was in any way prejudiced because he relied on the Pre-Trial brief, or Pre-Trial disclosure documents to formulate his Defence, once it proceeded at trial, he had the right to seek an adjournment. That's the first issue for the preparation of his Defence. As I think Judge Robinson pointed out, the appellant did not seek an adjournment, and as I'm sure you are aware from the transcripts, the Presiding Judge, Judge Mumba, asked him whether he wanted an adjournment, and he declined an adjournment. So the next issue then is whether or not the evidence that was brought forward at trial, the evidence of the criminal conduct of the appellant, was at variance with the indictment. In other words, the complaint by the appellant is that the evidence at trial came out from the testimony of Witness A, with respect to criminal conduct by accused B in the presence of the appellant for which he was not charged. That was the complaint made at trial. Now, the Trial Chamber could have responded in three ways. The Trial Chamber could have said, first of all, the conduct is in relation to the transaction for which you have been charged, which is the interrogation, a count of torture, and a count of outrages upon personal dignity including rape, and the means by which you carried this out was an interrogation. And we know from the standard or the legal definition of interrogation - of torture that it's the questioning, i.e. the interrogation, and the use of physical abuse to try and obtain an answer or achieve some result. They didn't do that. The Trial Chamber did not say: It's part of the same transaction, you were given full notification that the charges were interrogation, a torture, and the means was interrogation. They didn't do that. The second thing the Trial Chamber could have done is they could have asked the Prosecution whether they wanted to amend the indictment to conform to the evidence. That was completely valid, could have been done, and then the appellant would have been allowed to seek an adjournment to properly prepare his Defence. The Trial Chamber didn't do that. The action taken by the Trial Chamber was the most beneficial to the accused at the time because it excluded a basis of liability and evidence of criminal conduct which, on the testimony of Witness A, was clear, that the appellant was in fact present during the criminal conduct, and was part of the criminal conduct by either aiding and assisting B or being part of the interrogation. The Trial Chamber limited the liability and specifically excluded this as a basis for which he could be found guilty under 25 and 26. The appellant therefore, in our submission, gets the benefit. The evidence is excluded, but he gets it in, as he wanted, and as he acknowledged this morning he wanted, because he specifically wanted to cross-examine on it, because it goes to the credibility of Witness

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was permitted, it was in, he did rely on it, because he relied on that portion, which was admitted, not relied on by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber did not rely on this evidence for the conviction. But it was permitted to go in as part of the background and relied on by the defendant in cross-examining the Witness A. In fact, he refers to a number of statements where she says different things to show that she's confused in the sequencing, and that goes to her credibility. What the result is, is that the only prejudice that can be alleged and is the only prejudice alleged by the appellant, is whether or not there was evidence which was supposed to be excluded for the purpose of conviction, whether that evidence was relied upon by the Trial Chamber for the conviction. And I think that's the point that Judge Robinson made towards the end, that it's not an issue of the sufficiency of the indictment, it's whether or not, because of the variation, the evidence that was entered resulted in his conviction. Let me deal with the alleged prejudice that the appellant has noted. The appellant initially indicated that there were rapes and sexual assault by the accused B, which took place in the large room. His submission, if I understand it, was that the rapes -- the rape only -- the rape only identified in the indictment was that in the second room, the pantry, with the continuation of the interrogation. He claims that this evidence came out and that the Trial Chamber referred to or somehow relied on the rapes and sexual assault by accused B. My understanding, if I am not incorrect, is that when Your Honour Judge Shahabuddeen put it to him, "Are you saying that the Trial Chamber relied on the rapes and sexual assault by accused B to convict your client?" He qualified his answer by saying, "No." What he relied on was that it was used in some manner for the concerted action, but I'll get back to that. With respect to the rapes and sexual assault by Accused B in the large room, when the appellant was present. If necessary, I would ask you to look at paragraph 124 of the factual findings. There is no reference whatsoever to this evidentiary matter, and paragraph 264 of the legal findings, as there is no reference whatsoever to the rapes or sexual assault in the large room, in the presence of the appellant. There is no reliance on the Trial Chamber on this at all. The Trial Chamber does not rely on this alleged prejudice by the -- the prejudice alleged by the appellant. The second alleged prejudice is that the Trial Chamber somehow relied on the testimony as a whole, the testimony as a whole that was supposed to be excluded, to find that since he was present from the beginning of the conduct of Accused B, this was evidence of concerted action. And the allegation, if I understand it correctly by the appellant, is that the findings of the Trial Chamber were that he was there throughout the whole time, he was present throughout all these acts that Accused B engaged in, which were supposed to be excluded by the Trial Chamber, and that is a demonstration or some evidence of concerted action. That was the allegation that was made, as the second form of prejudice. Once again, if you look at paragraph 124 of the judgement, the factual findings. The factual findings in paragraph 124 are almost duplicative of the indictment, which is paragraph 25 of the indictment. There is no reference in paragraph 124 to a concerted action ongoing from the time of the arrival of the accused, in light of all the conduct taking place and in light of all the action of Accused B. The wording in 124 relates to the cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment and threats, which is the substance of paragraph 25 of the indictment, in the course of her interrogation by the accused -- the purpose was to extract information -- and that the interrogation and the abuse by Accused B were parallel to each other. At no point in time is there any factual findings regarding concerted action from the beginning in relation to evidence which was allegedly or supposedly excluded. The legal findings on paragraph 264. If you look at the legal findings on paragraph 264, the facts relied on in the legal findings are very narrowly circumscribed. They relate to the interrogation, the rubbing of the knife over the inner thighs, the threat to cut out Witness A's private parts, and the threat to confront Witness A with Witness D. This is the substance of the charges for which he was indicted and for which he was tried. With respect, there are no legal findings that there was concerted action dependent on facts which were supposedly not to be relied on by the Trial Chamber. The third claim of prejudice by the appellant is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You say, Mr. Farrell, that the judgement does not present any conclusion based upon the accused having being present from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Having been present from the beginning, in concert with the Accused B through the rapes and sexual assaults committed by Accused B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That is the exclusion. That if you look at the motion on June 11, what the Defence counsel asked for in the motion, the words they used are, "sexual assaults and rapes by Accused B in the large room." And that's the substance upon which the motion is granted. That's what they determined to be excluded. They don't determine to be excluded anything related to the conduct alleged in paragraph 25 and 26. They say only evidence which is not related to. So, with respect, the Trial Chamber, in its judgement on paragraph 80 -- in paragraph 80, I'm sorry -- in paragraph 80 specifically refers to the fact that it will not look at evidence which has been excluded. I'm sorry. It's paragraph 81. The witness has testified, I am reading from paragraph 81, Your Honours: "The witness has testified that rapes and sexual abuse ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The last sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. I was just going to refer to the first part, where it identifies the part that is to be excluded, rapes and sexual assault by B, which is exactly what was in the motion of June 11th, and which is what the Trial Chamber did not do. And then, as you've indicated, Judge Shahabuddeen, the last sentence is: "The Trial Chamber will not consider evidence relating to rapes and sexual assault of Witness A in the presence of the accused other than those alleged in paragraph 25 and 26." In light of a very clear ruling by the Trial Chamber in its judgement, that this is the part which is not to be excluded, and not to be considered, which is consistent with its order, in my respectful submission, you can't read into the factual findings at paragraph 164 or the -- sorry, 124, or the -- you can't read into the legal findings either at paragraph 264, the evidence which the appellant now alleges he's been prejudiced by. It's not there. It's not referred to. And we have a specific paragraph which says to the contrary. The last claim of prejudice alleged in this morning's submission was that the appellant was convicted for the act of Accused B in that he held a knife to the throat of Witness A. If I recall, that was one of the comments he made. The Defence claimed that the specific allegation of holding a knife to her throat was found in paragraph 24 of the indictment, the previous counts for counts 9 to 11, and was not found in the counts for which the appellant was charged and convicted. If you refer to paragraph 24 of the indictment, which once again, in my respectful submission, is not even before you, but accepting that it's been referred to by the appellant, if you refer to paragraph 24 in the indictment, though there is evidence that he used a knife, there is no specific allegation in paragraph 24 that Accused B held a knife to the throat of Witness A. That's not true. There are general allegations of his conduct and general allegations that he used a knife, but not the one that the appellant alleges was clearly in 24 and somehow was imported into paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying. The Trial Chamber did in fact make findings of fact about the happenings in the large room, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Well, maybe it's the choice of the words "finding of fact," Your Honour. There were findings of fact under paragraph 124, which are the factual findings of the judgement which refer to the specific acts in the large room that they find for the purpose of the conviction and, as I've already referred to Your Honour in paragraph 264, are the legal findings and the facts they rely on. The references that my friend has referred to regarding the large room, primarily are in the paragraphs which are the recitation of the facts in the first part of the judgement. When the -- when the Trial Chamber refers to the evidence -- if I can just find it. It would be of assistance. When the Trial Chamber refers to specific pieces of evidence, that's in the recitation of the facts. And, with respect, it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- is just part of the narrative?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try and find the reference. I remember seeing it earlier. But the one particular reference that is made starts off in this regard. It starts off with: "Witness A recalled ..." And then it continues the paragraph and then it talks about the testimony of Witness A in this regard. This is not part of the factual findings, with respect, and it is under the evidence that was presented at trial. That's the only reference to the knife in the judgement, and it's in the recitation of the facts and the narrative, in my submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You were not counsel in that case at the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I was not. With respect to this allegation that he was prejudiced because he was found guilty as to the knife to the throat, I'll just make two points on that. The first is that the indictment must set out the concise statement of the facts and the crime. It's to set out, as you are fully aware under Article 18, the identity of the victim, the place and the approximate date of the alleged offence, and the means by which the offence was committed. The material facts are set out in the indictment. It identifies the accused specifically; it identifies the victim specifically; it identifies a very narrow period of time; it identifies the counts of torture; and the outrages upon personal dignity; it identifies the means, which is the interrogation; and it notes the point about the rubbing of the knife by Accused B. This is an illustrative point of the interrogation, and also is used for the demonstration that there is concerted action. The evidence of the knife to the throat is just that, in our submission; it's evidence. The indictment does not have to set out every piece of evidence which forms the interrogation and the means by which the interrogation is carried out. And even if the Trial Chamber relied on it -- the Trial Chamber didn't, by the way, and I'll get to that. Even if the Trial Chamber relied on the knife to the throat as a basis for the conviction, in my respectful submission, that would be completely appropriate. The indictment deals with a particular act and a particular conduct and the material facts are set out. If there are things that take place during that interrogation, that doesn't require an amendment of the indictment, that's the evidence which supports the allegations of the indictment. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: In other words, you rely on the customary distinction between the facts alleged in the indictment and the evidence relating to the facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. My last point on this third piece of evidence which allegedly prejudiced the appellant, the appellant alleges once again that the Trial Chamber relied on evidence which was outside the scope of the indictment. Our submission, it was clearly within the scope of the indictment. In any event, the Trial Chamber never relied on it. There's no reference to the knife to the throat of the victim in the legal findings or the factual findings. Once again, I have cited the paragraphs, but there's no reference to it. The only reference to the knife to the throat is in the narrative or the recitation of facts. The conclusion on this ground of appeal, then, is that the specific concerns which the appellant raised for the majority of his submissions this morning regarding the indictment and his historical presentation of what happened at trial were remedied by the Trial Chamber in its decision. I've submitted that they could have found other means by which this evidence might have been admitted by amending the indictment, but the Trial Chamber decided in the circumstances, and that's not under dispute, that they would exclude the evidence which was at variation from the indictment. With respect to any concerns about being unable to prepare, the appellant never sought an adjournment when he was specifically asked, and said he was intending to proceed. The only complaint, after all of this, that the appellant brings forward at this stage is pieces of evidence which he claims the Trial Chamber relied on, and I've hopefully demonstrated in my submissions to you that the Trial Chamber did not rely on the evidence he alleged and specifically made a ruling and referred to that ruling in its judgement, that it would not rely on evidence outside of the scope in the indictment and in conformity with its order. If I may proceed, then, to the next ground I'd like to address. The next ground relates to the denial of a fair trial in light of the alleged conflicting testimony, and the two points referred to by the appellant this morning were, first of all, the conflicting testimony as to whether the appellant was present in the pantry, and the conflicting testimony with respect to whether or not the appellant interrogated A and D. This is formulated in the appellant's brief, if I understand it correctly, as a misapprehension of the evidence, that the Trial Chamber misapprehended the evidence of Witness D on whether or not the appellant was present in the pantry. And the second is that whether he was the interrogator, it's formulated as a failure of the Trial Chamber to give reasons on a decisive point. On the first, which is the misapprehension of the evidence as to whether the appellant was present in the pantry, it's set out in our brief, and I won't go through it now, that this is alleged as an error of fact; in other words, the Trial Chamber was in error, they made a mistake about the evidence, they made a mistake about whether he was present, because they found that he was present. This is an error of fact, and the onus is on the appellant to demonstrate that no reasonable trier of fact could have found that the appellant was present in the pantry. That would normally be the end of my submissions on this, because Witness A specifically stated he was in the pantry and specifically stated that he was there and committed the interrogation. But that's not the end of it. That would be sufficient evidence upon which a trier of fact could reasonably conclude that he was there. A witness testified to this fact and was cross-examined. In fact, if you check the transcripts, you'll see that at one point in time, Defence counsel at trial does not cross-examine Witness A on whether he was present, and Judge May at the trial said, "If you're going to allege -- if your defence is that he was not present, you at least have to put it to the witness so you can confront the witness and hear their testimony." The Defence counsel then, under the encouragement of Judge May, put it to the witness. "Isn't it true that the appellant was not present in the pantry during the interrogation?" And Witness A categorically states, "The appellant was present throughout." What her testimony is is that he was there when they entered and that he was near the door during the conduct, the assaults by Accused B. In my respectful submission, that's sufficient evidence upon which a trier of fact could decide, if they believed Witness A and if she was credible, that was sufficient evidence to say that the Trial Chamber could conclude that they were present in the pantry. But if I may, let me just refer to a few references in the transcripts. Witness D, as you'll recall, was brought to the small room as a means to confront Witness A. This is no coincidence that Witness D and Witness A are there, and this was specifically in light of the claim by the appellant, by the appellant, not by Accused B, by the appellant that, "If you do not answer our questions, we will confront you with a witness that will cause you to answer our questions." So you can't simply look at the step when they are standing in the pantry. You have to look at the reason for which they are there. The appellant specifically sets this up, specifically threatens Witness A, and then Witness A is taken to the room, and Witness D testifies that Accused B came and got him, and on his way down, they met with the appellant and they entered the room. To claim that the appellant was not there, was not in the room, seemingly didn't know what was going on and just seemed to be watching, negates the very purpose for which they were brought to the room. It negates the very purpose for which Appellant said, "I'm going to confront you."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Does it go as far as that? Is learned counsel for the other side taking his submission as far as that or is he merely saying that one is not consistent with the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, in -- my apologies. Not consistent in what way, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, there's a theory that the accused was not present in the pantry. Your submission is that his -- that that assertion negates the fact that in the large room, he told Witness A, "Look, if you don't cooperate, we will confront you with the other witness in the pantry." Is it a question of negation or consistency?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Possibly consistency then. But let me rephrase it then. The purpose for which Witness A is brought and Witness D is brought informs the trier of fact of the reason they are there and who's there. It's one piece of evidence which is consistent with his being there. I accept your qualification, though, Your Honour. So we start from that piece of evidence, which informs the trier of fact of the purpose for which they are there. We then look at Accused D's testimony. The appellant alleges in his brief that the only people in the pantry were Witness A, Accused B, and himself. If you go through the testimony of Witness D specifically, Witness D says, "I was brought by Accused B, the appellant, and another soldier," I think he says, "to this small room, the pantry." Witness D is then specifically asked, "Did you enter the room?" He said, "Yes, we entered the room, we all entered the room." That "all" can only be read as one thing, all the people that he was with, which includes Mr. Furundzija. Then the great discrepancy that my friend alludes to is the fact that he claims to be outside the door. In light of the purpose for which they are brought, in light of the fact that he brought D with Accused B in, in light of the fact that Accused D [sic] says, "He entered into the room with us when we entered, but then he was subsequently standing at the doorway, and he was in the doorway and he could see everything that was happening," for all intents and purposes, the accused was present throughout, and the evidence is not inconsistent in that regard and it is not something that a reasonable trier of fact couldn't have found. I'll just refer to paragraph 128 in the judgement, and it's a reference to the Accused B's conduct in the pantry. The second sentence begins: "The accused was present in the room as he carried out his interrogations. When not in the room, he was present in the near vicinity, just outside an open door, and he knew that crimes, including rape, were being committed." This is clearly the resolution or the way that the Trial Chamber resolves this issue of exactly where was he. He was clearly there, entered the room, on both witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me put it to you this way: Somebody said he was outside of the room. Witness A said he was inside the room. Did anybody say he was standing in the doorway?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: In fact, Witness A indicates that he was standing at the doorway, just inside the room at the doorway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So it was open to the Trial Chamber to find accordingly; is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Absolutely. It's clear that there's probably a space of about one foot between the threshold of the door and the doorway, and both witnesses place him at almost exactly the same spot. And the Trial Chamber finds accordingly. I'll now make my submissions on the failure of the Trial Chamber to give reasons or to address the alleged contradictory evidence regarding the interrogation. The submissions of the appellant appear to be, if I understand them correctly, that Accused A [sic] says that the appellant was the interrogator, that at various points in time he asked questions -- I'm now speaking about the pantry -- that he asked questions in the pantry. The appellant's position is that this was directly contradicted by Accused B [sic], who claims that the appellant never asked any questions in the pantry, and that as a result of the Trial Chamber's reliance on the issue of interrogation in the pantry, the questioning, as part of its findings of fact, that this creates such a clear and glaring contradiction that the failure to address it is an error of law. Before getting to the issue of whether they should or should not have addressed it, the Prosecution's submission is that this is not -- this characterisation of the evidence, in our respectful submission, is going a bit too far. The evidence of Witness D is that he was brought into the room and he was beaten, there was a beating going on. At this point in time, Accused A [sic] was not being beaten, and it appears, though it's not clear, but it appears that -- I think it's fair that it's Accused B that's beating Witness D in the room, with the appellant just at the doorway. The question is: "While you were being beaten, do you recall if anything was said while it was going on?" I'm merging two questions, but the question was: "Where was this lady," and this is Witness A, "while you were being beaten; do you know?" His answer is: "She was inside." Question: "Do you recall if anything was said while this was going on?"
