Answer: "No." This question: "Do you recall if anything was said whilst this was going on," was in relation to his being beaten. It's not in relation to the overall activities which took place in the room, it's not in relation to the time frames when Witness A was being beaten, and it cannot be interpreted as being a statement that nothing was said and no questions were asked when he was in the pantry. It says: "Do you recall if anything was said?" This is not a question about Mr. Furundzija, this is not a question of whether the appellant asked any questions. This is a question of whether there was a corresponding interrogation at the same time he was being beaten. That's what the question is about, in my respectful submission. The question -- on the next page of the transcripts, there is a question which says something along the lines: "Did the beatings continue?" And he says, in respect to the beatings against himself: "No, because the Accused B turned and started interrogating Witness A." Well, if this statement is to be read that nothing was ever said during the time he was there, that can't be correct, because his next question and answer is that: "After the beating against me stopped, interrogation started against Witness A." So therefore there were questions that took place in the pantry. He only identified Accused B as the one asking the questions. That's fair enough. But he does not state that Furundzija never asked any questions, and he's never asked that. In fact, he's never confronted with the question as to whether or not Furundzija ever asked any questions. He was not asked that in cross-examination, and he was not asked that despite, in my respectful submission, Judge May's comments to the Defence counsel just the day before, with respect to Witness A, that, "You have to confront the witnesses with respect to your defence to allow them to answer to it." When you look at it in light of what happened, there was one question on a particular issue regarding when he was beaten. In my respectful submission, there is not an inconsistency or a glaring contradiction here. The issue is not addressed. That's the submission of the Prosecution. And as the issue was not addressed, there's no failure of the Trial Chamber not to give reasons on a particular issue which was not addressed, was not confronted, was not part of the cross-examination, and was not put to Witness D. What you're left with, then, is Witness D saying, "During the time I was beaten, no one asked me any questions; i.e., there was no corresponding interrogation at the time I was beaten." And that's as far as it goes. That's not a contradiction to anything Witness A says in relation to the questions by Furundzija. Then you have Witness A stating that there was an interrogation. She does state that there was an interrogation of Witness D at one point in time, she does say that the questions by Furundzija were with respect to both of them, but she doesn't identify that the questions asked of Witness D were during his beating. She just indicates that there were questions asked of Witness D and Witness A by Furundzija as part of the interrogation. It's completely logical and the inference can be drawn that there are periods of silence by the inquisitor for the purpose of the continuing beating, to see whether it will get a reaction and then the interrogation might start. There's nothing inconsistent with the manner in which this took place or the answer of Witness D on this issue. If there is something that's there, it certainly doesn't rise to the level of a glaring inconsistency which would result in an error of law by the Trial Chamber for failing to give reasons. In my respectful submission, the Trial Chamber gave ample reasons. They tried to address the material before them. They specifically dealt with the section on the inconsistencies in Witness A's testimony. They refer to the fact that the Defence counsel raised complaints about Witness D's testimony, though not this one specifically, and, in my respectful submission, their reasons are quite lucid on their findings. Those are my submissions on whether or not the evidence is inconsistent or contradictory to the point that would require reasons. If I may, I'll now, well, first of all, speed up but not talk faster, but I would like to just deal with the admission of the evidence of Witness F, the witness who we now call Witness F, and Witness Surkovic, which are two -- there's two issues here. The first issue is the material filed before you, the affidavit, and the second issue is whether the Trial Chamber erred in excluding that material, if I may. Just to be clear, the Prosecution's submission is that this fresh evidence -- this affidavit of Witness F is fresh evidence and falls under Rule 115 and should not be admitted. Defence counsel may refer you to the fact that he filed a motion in June 1999 to this Appeals Chamber, asking to supplement the record on appeal. On July 20th, 1999, the Prosecution response to that dealt with two issues: the evidence he wanted to submit, which is the evidence regarding Judge Mumba; the material that was before the Bureau that he asked to be brought over before the appeal. The Prosecution also noted in there that he had filed an affidavit before the Appeals Chamber and indicated that he should meet Rule 115 before that affidavit is admitted before the Appeals Chamber. The order of the Appeals Chamber on September 2nd states that the motion to supplement the record is granted, but the wording is that, "... considering that Rules 115 and 119 of the Rules are not applicable to the material sought to be admitted, which pertains to the appellant's ground of appeal concerned with the partiality of a Judge at trial and not with guilt or innocence of the appellant." With respect, the order of the Appeals Chamber was specifically with respect to the request of the Defence counsel, which was to supplement the record on the evidence regarding Judge Mumba. The reply of the Prosecution raises this additional issue and says the Prosecution's position is he must bring a motion. No motion was brought. In fact -- I'm sorry, Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell, it is possible that I misapprehend the course of the arguments, and certainly there has been a factor of evolution involved, but at this moment I have the impression that your learned friend on the other side is not taking the position -- if I'm wrong, he can correct me -- that this affidavit statement of the witness is being submitted as additional evidence. My understanding of his purpose is this: that he is merely submitting the affidavit as an indication of the type of evidence which he says was erroneously excluded by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have two -- I think you're absolutely right, and it's my submission that that's exactly his point, that it's not new evidence. And my response to that is two-fold: One, the question that this Appeals Chamber must decide is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you. Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. The issue before this Appeals Chamber is whether or not the Trial Chamber erred on the evidence which was before it and whether the evidence and material filed before the Trial Chamber satisfied the purpose for admission of evidence on the reopening. This evidence is irrelevant to your function, which is to determine whether or not the Trial Chamber erred on the material before it in excluding evidence. That's why it should not be before you. My second point is that though he claims this is not new evidence, with respect, there are three pieces of evidence which are in this affidavit which are not in the material before the Trial Chamber, and that clearly makes it fresh evidence. The evidence is -- there's additional evidence on the character of the accused in the affidavit before you, there's additional evidence on her condition at the time in the affidavit before you, and there's additional evidence that this person, Witness F, claims that he met a person who Witness A refers to as Muflon, and then he describes that this Muflon is approximately 172 centimetres tall and had light brown to blonde hair. This is filed two days before the appellant's brief. This affidavit is dated June 23rd, 1999. It's filed two days before the appellant's brief, which raises the ground of appeal that there's a failure in the -- frailty in the identification evidence by Witness A with respect to Mr. Furundzija. This has nothing to do with the reopening, this evidence was not before the Trial Chamber in the material filed as the summation of the evidence, and this is clearly fresh evidence which is improperly before you. And as my friend has acknowledged, this is not fresh evidence, and therefore this whole affidavit should be excluded from your consideration, and the consideration, in my respectful submission, is whether or not the Trial Chamber, on the material filed before it, erred. That is why, as you'll recall, the Prosecution brought an application in August of this year to ask that the documents which were filed regarding this application to admit evidence -- they were filed ex parte at trial. At trial, the Prosecution had no idea about this witness -- I'm sorry, had no idea -- not about the witness, I apologise -- the Prosecution had no idea about the application to bring this witness forward for the reopening. It was filed ex parte. On a determination as to whether or not the Trial Chamber erred in excluding it, the Prosecution, as I've said, is not content to go on an affidavit with new evidence but wants to see whether the Trial Chamber erred. As a result, there was an order by this Appeals Chamber in September, September 2nd, 1999, lifting the ex parte status of the material filed before the Chamber, and access has been granted to the Prosecution. That's the material that the Prosecution relies on to say that the Trial Chamber did not err, because on the material before them, many of these factual statements that are in the affidavit were not before the Trial Chamber. If I can just refer to the particular evidence in the material, there's only one piece of evidence in the material that was before the Trial Chamber that had anything to do with medical matters, if I can put it that way. In the defendant's request before the Trial Chamber, most of the evidence is evidence which, in our submission, is evidence which the Defence could have obtained before trial. It was evidence which the Witness A testified to. You will recall that Witness A spoke about Witness F, the man from a particular place, as where she stayed before she was exchanged immediately after being released. Well, as ineffectiveness or incompetence of counsel is not being raised, this was obviously evidence which was clearly of some relevance to Witness A. She testified to where she stayed afterwards, and she specifically referred to the individual himself. If the Defence counsel felt it was necessary at that point in time to obtain evidence from this individual, Witness F, or to ask for an adjournment to seek out whether or not it was someone who they would like to bring before the Court, then the obligation was on them at the time to do it at the time. If you refer to the document filed before the Trial Chamber, almost all of it is in reference to identification issues, character, and the comments made by Witness A to Witness F at the time she stayed at his house before she was -- after she was released and before she was exchanged to go to Zenica. There's two references. One is that during the time that she was at Witness F's house, she was clothed, fed, and received medical attention until her exchange. And the other is that Witness A -- sorry, Witness F believed that Witness A was on the edge of insanity and that she had confided in him that she was suicidal. With respect, this has nothing to do with treatment or counselling, it has nothing to do with the issue regarding the reopening, and the Trial Chamber clearly did not err. The Prosecution's position is essentially the same with respect to the witness Surkovic. Clearly, the Defence counsel was fully aware of it, and in fact the Defence counsel cross-examined Witness A on the Surkovic -- the statement that was allegedly taken by Surkovic. It's not a case where the Witness A denies that she met or spoke with Surkovic. She denies in her testimony that it was her signature on the statement. That's the issue. She doesn't deny that she spoke with Mr. Surkovic and that she told him certain things. That is clearly before the Trial Chamber. She was cross-examined on it, and it was a matter that was dealt with during Witness A's testimony. Once again, in my respectful submission, there is no issue with respect to the Trial Chamber's exclusion of this evidence. In light of our comments that we would finish by 3.45, I have been tasked to address other issues in relation to grounds 1, 2 and 3, so not the ground related to Judge Mumba, not the ground related to sentence. If there is any questions on those grounds, I'll attempt to be of assistance. If not, I'll allow my colleague at least 15 minutes to address you on the sentencing ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Your colleague may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: May it please the Chamber, the Prosecution's detailed response to the appeal against sentence is contained in the Prosecution response brief. I would confine myself merely to a few supplementary submissions. The first relates to the standard of review by the Appeals Chamber in an appeal against a sentence. That is dealt with in paragraph 7.5 to 7.7 of our response brief. The Prosecution position is that the standard of review is an abuse of discretion standard; that the Appeals Chamber should not interfere with the sentence imposed by a Trial Chamber merely because the Appeals Chamber feels that a different sentence would be more appropriate. The discretion in relation to sentencing matters, we submit, is that of the Trial Chamber and not of the Appeals Chamber, and that the Appeals Chamber would only grant an appellate remedy if the Trial Chamber erred either on matters of law prejudicing the convicted person or if the Trial Chamber has gone beyond the scope of its legitimate discretion. In relation to that, I would now draw the Appeals Chamber's attention to relevant parts of the Tadic sentencing appeal, which was decided on the 26th of January this year, which was after our response brief was filed. In paragraph 20 of that judgement there is a passage at which the Appeals Chamber says that it could find no error in the exercise of the Trial Chamber's discretion in imposing the sentence that it did, and that it would therefore not quash the sentence that was imposed, and substitute its own instead. There is a similar reference in those terms in paragraph 21, and again in paragraph 73 of that judgement. So we would submit that since our response brief was filed, we now have authority of this Appeals Chamber for the standard of review for which we are contending. The question then is whether an abuse of discretion has been established by the appellant in this case. And we say that the burden is on the appellant to establish that. The alleged error set out in the appellant's brief is the allegation that the sentence imposed in this case was inconsistent with what the appellant refers to as the emerging penal regime of the International Tribunal. And if one looks at the argument in the appellant's brief, what it essentially does is take the various sentences that have been imposed by this Tribunal in different cases, in relation to different crimes, and seeks to extrapolate from that some kind of -- one could call them almost mathematical principles, which it is then claimed are the governing sentencing principles in this Tribunal. The conclusion, as a result of that analysis, is set out on page 155 of the appellant's brief. The formula which the appellant seeks to derive from this analysis is that the maximum sentence that can be imposed by this Tribunal in relation to a war crime is nine years. And it seems that that submission is put by the appellant, regardless of the nature of the war crime. Indeed a reference is made to the Erdemovic case, and the suggestion is that even a war crime involving the killing of 70 people would lead to a maximum sentence of nine years. I would submit that is a proposition that would only need to be stated to be rejected. The appellant's brief then goes somewhat further and says that if the war crime in question does not lead to the death of the victim, that it must be discounted by three years, so that the maximum sentence that could be imposed in this case is six years. The Prosecution submits that there are a number of fundamental errors in this kind of analysis. The first is that the samples taken in this analysis are relatively few in number. They involve a variety of different crimes, committed by a variety of different accused, with different personal factors and different aggravating and mitigating circumstances. And the Prosecution would submit that from that small sample, one couldn't seek to derive principles that would be of general application in all cases. Secondly, and more importantly, the decisions relied on are principally decisions of Trial Chambers. In fact, they were all decisions of Trial Chambers, apart from the one reference to the Erdemovic appeal. But the Erdemovic appeal, of course, was not concerned with sentencing principles. It was concerned with the issue of the validity of a plea of guilty, and it's submitted that doesn't provide any guidance in relation to sentencing matters. The difficulty with relying on decisions of Trial Chambers, of course, is that they are not binding on the Appeals Chamber. Indeed, some Trial Chambers have expressed the view that they are not binding on other Trial Chambers. A further difficulty still is that many of these decisions of Trial Chambers are presently the subject of pending appeals. In fact, most of the sentences imposed, both by this Tribunal and the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, are the subject of pending appeals. And, of course, the Appeals Chamber couldn't take, as a reference point in one case, a sentence subject to appeal in another case without prejudging a pending appeal in another case. Thirdly, and even more importantly still, we would submit, the problem with this analysis is that it's undermined by certain recent decisions of this Appeals Chamber. The appellant, for instance, places reliance on the Trial Chamber's decision in Aleksovski, and says that the Aleksovski Trial Chamber sentence is entirely consistent with the International Tribunal's emerging penal regime. The Appeals Chamber will be aware that the sentence in that case has now been revised by the Appeals Chamber, last month, thereby undermining the appellant's theory of what the supposed emerging penal regime is. The appellant's analysis also relies on the proposition that an act performed as a crime against a humanity is, all else being equal, more serious than the same act committed as a war crime, and that proposition must now also be regarded as incorrect, in light of the Tadic sentencing appeal. The proposition that the maximum sentence for a war crime is nine years is also contradicted by the recent Tadic sentencing appeal, since the Appeals Chamber in that case revised sentences and ultimately pronounced sentences of 20 years for wilful killings under Article 2, and murders under Article 3. And finally, the analysis undertaken by the appellant is not, in fact, even supported by some of the Trial Chamber decisions cited. The appellant's brief appears to concede that the sentences imposed on one of the accused in the Celebici case for counts 18 to 20 were inconsistent with the calculations in the appellant's brief. And yet, for the reasons given in the Prosecution's response brief, we would submit that that is in fact the sentence probably most closely analogous, on its facts, to the circumstances of this case. The Prosecution doesn't take issue with the general proposition that the Appeals Chamber should establish general sentencing guidelines in order to achieve consistency and evenhandedness, but these principles will have to be established by the Appeals Chamber itself, for the guidance of Trial Chambers, rather than vice versa, rather than the suggestion that the Appeals Chamber take as guidance the sentences that have been handed down by Trial Chambers to date. The Prosecution response brief sets out what the Prosecution submits are the appropriate sentencing principles in this Tribunal. And I needn't repeat all that is there. I do draw the Chamber's attention to the fact that similar submissions were made by the Prosecution in the appeal against sentence in the Aleksovski case. The Prosecution appeal in that case has now been upheld in an oral judgement by the Appeals Chamber, so, in a sense, these submissions have already been ruled upon by a differently constituted Appeals Chambers, although no reasons for decision have been given in that yet. So it's not possible to tell to what extent or on what basis. I also draw the Appeals Chamber's attention to the fact that similar submissions have also been put in the written briefs in the Celebici case, the Celebici appeal by the Prosecution. I am not suggesting that the Appeals Chamber should go beyond the scope of the submissions in this case, but clearly the issue of these general principles is one of general importance in the practice of the Tribunal as a whole. The Prosecution submissions as to what the applicable principles are start with the premise that the main purpose of sentencing in this Tribunal is deterrence. And we identify two main aspects to deterrence: what we call the suppressive aspect, which is probably what is traditionally understood as deterrence, and the educative aspect, which is the international community's expression of revulsion and condemnation of these crimes and its refusal to tolerate them. In our brief we also refer to the purpose of retribution. It may be that this is synonymous with -- or overlaps considerably with - what we describe as this educative aspect. We note also that some decisions of Trial Chambers have also identified other purposes of sentencing, including protection of society, stigmatisation, and reconciliation and restoration of peace in the former Yugoslavia. We would submit that to the extent that these may be recognised as valid purposes of sentencing in this Tribunal, they can generally be subsumed under the broader concept of deterrence, as we've defined it. What we would, however, submit is that despite references to rehabilitation as a factor in decisions of some Trial Chambers, this cannot be a primary purpose of sentencing in this Tribunal. National criminal justice systems generally have a much wider range of sentencing options, including fines, community service orders, parole and supervised release, enabling rehabilitation to be a more prominent factor. The Tribunal doesn't have these options, yet the Tribunal was established, despite the limited sentencing options that it would have, to deal with these crimes precisely because of their very seriousness, and the purpose of the Tribunal is to deter them. In relation to this general premise, I draw attention to paragraph 48 of the recent Tadic sentencing appeal, where it's said by the Appeals Chamber that it's accepted the deterrence may legitimately be considered in sentencing, but that it should not be accorded undue prominence in the overall assessment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: That finding is not elaborated on in detail in that judgement. And it may be a matter of some interpretation as to what "undue prominence" would be. Presumably, if deterrence were the only consideration in sentencing, one would always impose the highest sentence in every case because this would have the greatest deterrent effect, and we would concede, of course, that would be giving undue prominence to deterrence as a factor. We would submit that the finding of the Appeals Chamber in that case is not necessarily inconsistent with the position being put by the Prosecution. The Prosecution position is that sentencing must begin with an assessment of the gravity of the crime and take account of individual factors, and on that basis, it's submitted that seeing deterrence as the primary purpose of sentencing is not to give it undue prominence in the assessment of what the actual sentence is. On the subject of the Tadic sentencing appeal, I should also draw attention to the finding of the Appeals Chamber there at paragraphs 51 to 58, in which one of the appellant's grounds of appeal was upheld relating to the need to develop a range of sentences based upon the relative position of the accused. In that case the Appeals Chamber said that although the criminal conduct of the convicted person was incontestably heinous, the accused's level in the command structure, when compared to that of commanders, was low, and this justified a reduction of sentences of 25 and 24 years to 20 years. The Prosecution submits that this finding is also not inconsistent with the position put by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: It relates to another principal point made in the Prosecution brief, which is that sentences imposed by this Tribunal should not generally be lower than the type of sentences that would be imposed by a national court in respect of similar conduct for a crime committed under national law. If that were the case, the message to the international community would be that a particular act, if committed as a war crime, or a crime against humanity, is somehow a lesser offence than the same conduct when committed as a crime under national law. It's accepted then that crimes of different gravity should in principle receive sentences of different gravity, but there comes a point at which - that must cease to be meaningful. If a person has committed a crime warranting the maximum sentence available, one assumes circumstances that -- say 100 victims were killed; one can't discount that sentence from the maximum to allow room for other perpetrators who might have killed 1.000 or 2.000 victims. The same comment applies in relation to the relative level of perpetrators. It may be, and we make this point in our brief, that where a person orders or plans a large-scale crime, the culpability, the gravity of that perpetrator's conduct, may be greater than that of individual perpetrators, because individual perpetrators are responsible for the particular crimes they commit, whereas the planner or instigator may be responsible for the crimes of many. But in the case of an individual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was interested in what you said earlier about comparison with national practice. Did you have in mind any particular country, or are you just speaking generally?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, the Statute and the Rules do mandate that the Trial Chambers have regard to the practice of the courts in the former Yugoslavia. And this is a matter that is routinely taken into account by Trial Chambers. I think there has always been a practical difficulty in that respect, because the sentencing practice of the courts in the former Yugoslavia is not just a matter of ascertaining what the legislation was, but what the actual practice of the courts was. And that may be a matter of difficult research. But if it's also accepted that the crimes within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal are international crimes, that they apply universally in all countries, there would be a certain arbitrariness as well, if the punishment imposed for such crimes could vary widely, depending on different national jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's what I had in mind, whether you are able to point to any trial in a particular country relating to this kind of case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Our submission would be, Your Honour, that this Tribunal can't be bound to the national provisions of any one country. It's also accepted that when one refers to national legal systems generally, it's very hard to make comparisons, because there may be wide divergences between the types of sentences that would be imposed from one country to another for exactly the same conduct. What I have submitted, perhaps, is a very general sort of comparison to the types of sentences one would normally expect in a national jurisdiction. It's perhaps harder to say much more than that, other than that one recognises, when one sees a sentence that seems very low, compared to what would normally be given in a national jurisdiction for the same conduct. This also relates to the discretion of the Trial Chamber, that if there are considerable variations in the types of sentences that would be imposed by national courts, this reflects the range of discretion that a Trial Chamber would have in matters of sentencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would it be all right, Mr. Staker, if we were to extend your time by five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I would be very appreciative, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Bench agrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution submits that when these principles are applied to the facts of this case, the appellant has established no abuse of discretion by the Trial Chamber. It must be expected that the crimes of which the accused was convicted would be treated as very serious crimes in a national legal system. As the Trial Chamber found, torture is one of the most serious offences known to international law. That was stated at paragraph 281 of the Trial Chamber's judgement. Additionally, the Trial Chamber noted various aggravating factors. In the Tadic sentencing appeal, the Appeals Chamber affirmed that the Tribunal is not bound by the 20-year maximum or any 20-year maximum under the law of the former Yugoslavia. Under the express terms of Rule 101(A) of the rules of this Tribunal: "A convicted person may be sentenced to imprisonment for a term up to and including the remainder of the convicted person's life." And although it's submitted that sentences imposed by Trial Chambers can't be a point of reference before this Appeals Chamber, we do note that in several cases before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, sentences for the remainder of the convicted person's life have been imposed on six persons, and that in the Jelisic case before this Tribunal, a sentence of 40 years was imposed. And viewed in the context of that sentencing range, the Prosecution submits that the overall 10-year sentence imposed in this case can't be considered even anywhere near the high end of the sentencing scale. And it's submitted, on that basis, that the appellant has demonstrated no abuse of discretion by the Trial Chamber. I would finally just refer to one other argument which is developed in the appellant's reply brief and was also mentioned orally this morning, which is to the effect that, in view of the inconsistencies and uncertainty of the evidence, there ought to be some mitigation to take account of that factor. The Prosecution's submission would be that this is simply inconsistent with basic principles of criminal law. The Trial Chamber has to determine whether guilt is proved beyond a reasonable doubt, and if the evidence is so inconsistent and uncertain that there is a reasonable doubt, the accused will be convicted. And if the Trial Chamber finds that the guilt has been proved beyond a reasonable doubt, then sentencing must be based on the facts, as found by the Trial Chamber. What the appellant seems to be suggesting is that an accused might be convicted where there are doubts, but those doubts would then be taken into account by imposing a lower sentence, and the Prosecution would submit that that is an inadmissible argument. Unless I can be of further assistance, they are the submissions of the Prosecution on the sentencing appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Chamber is grateful to you. We will now suspend and we'll return at 10 minutes past 4.00 to hear you for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I hope I can respond to all of that in 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: This sitting is resumed. Mr. Misetic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I too will try to be quick, but slow-paced for the translators in the booth. I'm going to first try to address the response -- respond to the Prosecution presentation point by point in the order that they did, and then my concluding remarks. First, the issue of standard of review was raised and that the standard of review allegedly is that the Appeals Chamber can only look to see whether there is a reasonable basis to make this conclusion. We obviously fundamentally disagree with that. It's against the overwhelming case law in common-law jurisdictions, and that is mostly where the standard of "beyond a reasonable doubt" comes from. Furthermore, in counsel's argument towards the end, when he discusses the Tadic decision to overturn -- the Tadic appellate decision to overturn a finding that there was reasonable doubt and they overturned it in favour of the Prosecution, counsel basically, in effect, admitted what the standard is, and I think that in his resumation of that standard, we would be in agreement, and that is that the standard of "beyond a reasonable doubt" is incorporated into that standard that first appears in the Tadic decision, and that is when you are analysing whether there is a reasonable basis to make this conclusion in the evidence, presumed or assumed into that standard is that you're looking to see whether there is a reasonable basis to make this conclusion that there was no reasonable doubt. Again, that is precisely what subsequently happens in the Tadic appellate decision. The Appellate Chamber finds that the Trial Chamber's decision that there was reasonable doubt was unreasonable, and so you do have the authority to review the evidence and determine whether or not a reasonable doubt existed. I hope you were able to follow that or I was able to articulate that, I hope. So, again we proceed on that basis, and we say that you need to review the evidence and to determine whether or not a reasonable doubt existed. From that point, counsel doesn't address what "reasonable doubt" is. They just say, "You can't look at reasonable doubt in this case," and so therefore I would submit to you that the extension then -- the more detailed analysis then is, "What is a reasonable doubt?" And again I don't think there is any disagreement with the Prosecution, in that the standard that they espoused for what "proof beyond a reasonable doubt" is in the Tadic appellate decision is precisely the exact same standard that I am arguing for now, which is you have to look to see whether there is a fair or rational inference of the evidence of innocence. In Tadic, they argued that there wasn't, and the Appellate Chamber agreed and convicted Tadic. In this case, we're arguing, "Apply the same standard, only looking at the evidence, you have to acquit because there is a fair or rational inference." I think our position on what the standard of appeal is is consistent with common law, and consistent with the Tadic appellate decision, and is precisely what the Tadic Appellate Chamber did in overturning the Trial Chamber's finding that there was reasonable doubt. I'm going to try to move quickly through these arguments. The issue with respect to Witness D. I find it unfortunate that there is some inference that we tried, through subterfuge or something like that, to insert an issue. The fact of the matter is it is in our appellate brief. We flushed it out more in the reply brief. We've had four months since the filing of the last pleading in this case, which was in November. We had no motion to strike that as an issue, we had no conference or communication between the parties on that issue, and this is the first I've heard an objection, and so I again say that it was raised in the briefs and we ask you to consider it. They turn then in response to our argument about sequencing, and it's not consistent with what happened at trial. First, there is this allegation that Judge Mumba put it to me that we could have some sort of a recess, and I've, in the break, tried to find where that exists. And at least on the date in question when we made the motion, I can't find that anywhere in the transcript. I do recall at approximately -- on the opening of the trial, prior to trial, Judge Mumba asked us if we wanted a recess, but it had nothing to do with any of the issues here. It had to do with the fact that the Prosecution was delinquent in discovery and turning over witness statements, and Judge Mumba had proposed that we delay the trial and take an adjournment. If I'm wrong, I trust that counsel will correct me. But as far as I can recall, and looking through my computer here, there was never an issue of Judge Mumba asking us if we wanted an adjournment, and indeed it is illogical that she would have done that, given that they granted our motion. Now, we've spent quite a lot of time on this issue of notice. There is no question as to what was alleged by the Prosecution, and in their appellate brief here, as I pointed out earlier, there is an admission that the pre-trial brief alleges that certain acts took place prior to the defendant's arrival. Now they are alleging that -- to be honest with you, I'm trying to still gather what exactly their position is, because they ignore the fact that all of the submissions they've made here on appeal were rejected by the Trial Chamber. So this argument that the indictment -- that, (A), that we're not allowed -- or that somehow counts 9, 10 and 11 don't apply to Mr. Furundzija, those arguments were addressed at trial because we raised it at the appropriate time, and they were addressed in our favour and against that very position that the Prosecutor now puts forward on appeal. And I would argue that in doing this through their response, they are indirectly appealing the Trial Chamber's orders of June 12 and June 15. All of these issues were litigated at trial. The fact of the matter is that our notice argument was accepted at trial. To the extent that we have re-raised the notice issue on appeal, it is because the Trial Chamber's failure to adhere to its own order then leads to two problems. One is that the admitted failure -- that the admitted inconsistency is with the indictment, and the admitted -- the Trial Chamber's admission that we would not have a fair trial, okay, raises back again the issue of whether or not we had fair notice in the indictment stage or, alternatively, raises the issue of whether or not then the Trial Chamber committed error in not adhering to its own order. If you look at the decision, the very decision that we're arguing about here is an order from the 12th of June, and it basically says as follows: "... hereby allows the oral motion and holds that in the circumstances, the Trial Chamber will only consider as relevant Witness A's evidence insofar as it relates to paragraphs 25 and 26 as pleaded in the indictment against the accused." Now, counsel has mischaracterised what the oral motion was, and I've retrieved it here and I would like to just put it to you as to what the conversation was between myself and Judge May as to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- as to what -- it says it's on. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. There is a point at page 507 of the trial transcript where I am arguing and I specifically tell the Court that, "If we are going to litigate the large room now, I'm going to have to travel back to the former Yugoslavia to find witnesses." And Judge May specifically asks -- and I'm sorry, here I'm working by myself, so -- here is the oral motion that the written order says was granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "Going back to the question I asked, though, what are you asking us to do?" My answer: "We are asking you to strike, to strike the portions of her testimony with respect to room 1. It can stay with respect to the pantry." That was the oral motion. And the written order then says: "The defendant's oral motion is granted." For the Prosecution's new argument now to say that this only applied with respect to the rape and that that wasn't taken into consideration ignores my oral motion and the written order saying that this oral motion was granted, and the oral motion was to strike the entire testimony. Now, I don't think there's an ambiguity in this in terms of what was the decision. The Prosecution is now claiming that there is an ambiguity here, at least arguing indirectly that there is an ambiguity. I would submit to you that if the Trial Chamber did not want to strike her testimony with respect to the large room, then this order should say: "... denies the Defence oral motion, but in the circumstances will exclude her testimony only about rape in the large room." But it doesn't say that. Again, so this is what we were relying on, and I again also ask you to consider what I had read earlier. "If the large room was at issue," I specifically said to the Court, "tell me, because then I need to take a break and I need to go down to Bosnia and start finding witnesses." Instead, all we got was this: "We grant the oral motion." So I stand on the ground of appeal for two reasons: one, the argument that they misled us, the Prosecution did, in terms of its indictment and pre-trial pleadings; and, two, that there was error in terms of not following the orders of the 12th and the 15th of June. The concerted action findings. Now, this -- I find the argument somewhat remarkable, but it appears that the argument is that the Trial Chamber recited certain facts, but then did not rely on those facts in convicting my client. The question I have for the Prosecution, then, is why go through the process of reciting the facts if you don't intend to rely on them? And furthermore, a fair reading of the judgement does not support that conclusion. Paragraph 108 of the judgement is the first paragraph under a section titled "Findings." Within that paragraph it says: "The Trial Chamber accepts her evidence ...", meaning Witness A's evidence, "... she has sufficiently recollected these material aspects of the events. So the Trial Chamber has accepted her testimony. Now we get to the factual findings, which is still within subpart 4 of findings. And it says: "Having considered the evidence, the Trial Chamber is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the following findings can be made." We'll skip the first part, because it's not relevant to the argument, but paragraph 123, towards the end: "She is brought to the Bungalow. Around her, the soldiers dressed in Joker uniforms, awaited the arrival of the man referred to as 'the boss.' Witness A then heard someone announce the arrival of Furundzija, and the man she identified, to the satisfaction of the Trial Chamber as being Anto Furundzija, the accused, entered the room, holding some papers in his hands." First, there is the first factual finding. He shows up first, in the judgement. 124: "Witness A was interrogated by the accused. She was forced by Accused B to undress and remain naked before a substantial number of soldiers." There is the first inconsistency with the indictment. She was forced to undress under all -- under the indictment and the pre-trial pleadings, well before Anto Furundzija was alleged to arrive. Indeed, she was forced to undress, she was threatened with a knife, et cetera, by Accused B, and then subsequently raped, multiple times, by Accused B before Mr. Furundzija is alleged to have arrived. This is the next sentence which I think clearly then incorporates all of the factual findings or the factual recitation prior to this. "She was subjected to cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment and to threats of serious physical assault by Accused B in the course of her interrogation by the accused." There we have the rest of it. This is a legal conclusion about cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment which incorporates the knife to the throat, et cetera. There is simply no other way of looking at the evidence. And the fact that all of these facts, which I put up on these boards and spent two hours going over with you, are recited by the Trial Chamber, and then in its findings of fact it, in an umbrella, says she was subjected to cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment. Any fair reading of this, then, would have you refer back to what the facts alleged are, to determine exactly what the Trial Chamber is talking about there. And I think it's clear, reading all of the evidence together, that these cruel, inhumane -- this cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment is the knife to the throat, forcing her to undress, et cetera. It goes on. The last sentence of that paragraph: "The interrogation by the accused and the abuse by Accused B were parallel to each other." This sentence falls within a finding in the large room. There can be -- now it's clear. He arrived first. She is then forced to undress at knife point, et cetera, during his interrogation. So there is no fair reading of this to support what they are trying to say, which is, "Yes, there are all these recitations of fact, but you have to confine yourself to these few paragraphs. And if it doesn't say it within these three paragraphs, then the Trial Chamber didn't rely on it." I don't think that that's a fair reading of the evidence. And I would again submit that it is clear that the Trial Chamber put him at the beginning of this sequence of events and then made certain conclusions on the basis of those findings; that he was there from the beginning, et cetera, et cetera. Even the finding that he left her in the custody of Accused B to be raped. Again, I don't see how that is consistent with the June 12th order. Even that -- and that finding alone, which says that it will not consider evidence of rape or sexual assault in the large room. Then why reference it at all? Instead there is a specific conclusion in the judgement that he did so. So again, the Defence rejects the conclusions that somehow he was not placed there at the beginning, that he was not responsible from the beginning for all of these acts that transpired, et cetera. Now, Witness D's testimony. Your Honour, to say that it is a stretch, their interpretation of Witness D's testimony is a stretch --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just one minute. I have before me the inadmissibility ruling of 15 June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, what you were referring to was some evidence to the effect that the accused left Witness A in the large room to be raped by Accused B. Is that the same thing as an act of rape committed in the presence of the accused in the large room?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There are clearly legal consequences found by the Trial Chamber in this judgement. What the extent of the difference is, is something that I have not thought about. But clearly, under either scenario, there are legal consequences for that conduct. And I would ask you to keep in mind the June 12th written ruling, which is also something that you should have in considering this. Does the Court have a copy of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where it says, "allows the oral motion and holds that in the circumstances the Trial Chamber will only consider as relevant Witness A's evidence insofar as it relates to paragraphs 25 and 26." Which is exactly what we had wanted. And we got it. And then finally I would say that it was clear what our point was. We had not yet put on our case in chief. If the large room was an issue, tell us, so that we can get evidence and put it on; that he was not in the large room; that none of this happened in his presence, et cetera. But we never got that opportunity. And that takes me back to that whole argument I made at the beginning about fairness. All we wanted was an opportunity to put on a defence. We didn't get that opportunity. We get these orders and then, at the end of the day, we find out that, although I had asked the Trial Chamber to let me know whether the large room was at issue, I was told no, and then the judgement said yes. That's the issue of fairness that I am talking about. And that's where we want the Appellate Chamber to intervene, if nothing else, to preserve some fairness to allow him to defend himself or to acquit him directly. This issue of Witness D. The Prosecution cites one question and one answer and takes it completely outside the context of the rest of that passage. There is no question what he is saying here. It starts on paragraph 347. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now we are going to try to stretch, try to place semantics with words, to try to read in a little possibility that maybe he meant he doesn't recall who was interrogating or whether anything was being said. I submit that that is clearly not an acceptable reading of the evidence. Furthermore, to clear up any ambiguity whatsoever, he gave a witness statement prior to trial. Now, that witness statement, from our perspective, was not in evidence. So we didn't use it in closing argument. However, in reviewing the judgement and preparing for this argument, I came to realise that the judgement makes nine footnotes to an exhibit called D8. D8 is Witness D's witness statement, which is not in evidence. So the Trial Chamber uses a statement not in evidence to support its judgement. From my perspective, that's fine. However, we should have known that this statement is fair game and we could argue it. Because if we could have argued it, and I think it's up to you to rule whether the Trial Chamber had committed error in relying on testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, can you help me. Are you referring to the judgement, to any particular part?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will cite the footnotes for the record. Footnote 102, footnote 107, footnote 109, footnote 114, footnote 116, footnote 119, footnote 120, footnote 121, footnote 126.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Which one refers to this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You need a copy of the Defence exhibits, but they all refer to Defence Exhibit 8 and Defence Exhibit 8 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see that in 102, Defence Exhibit 8. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I've got the drift of it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 8 is Witness D's witness statement. So they rely on evidence in the judgement. And this is not some attempt by me to mislead anyone. But in preparing for this, and looking at the footnotes, they rely on this statement. So again I leave it to you. If it's error, then it's error that requires a reversal. Because they have considered now within their deliberations evidence that's not admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Alternatively, though --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: How is it -- I am trying to reconcile two things. It's referred to here as Exhibit D8. I assume from that, that it was in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Nobody moved it into evidence. And if you look at the roster of exhibits -- if you look at the roster of exhibits, at least as was provided to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It was not tendered in evidence, but it was marked Exhibit D. Is that the point you are making?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. So it is not in evidence for consideration in the judgement. Now, if the Appellate Chamber were to rule that it is -- my point in all of this isn't to attack necessarily --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You wouldn't say that's a technical point, would you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I am saying is I anticipated or tried to anticipate that they were going to object to my reading the testimony of Witness D from the statement, and so I wanted to lay the foundation for why I am using this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So again, I would say, Your Honours, at the very least, we are owed an explanation as to how they were reconciling this testimony. Furthermore, we can't even start to assume what the testimony was, because we don't know what evidence that the Trial Chamber considered. We don't know what the basis of the conclusion was, whether it was trial testimony, whether it was this witness statement, et cetera. We again re-submit that that is a live issue and they should have considered it, and it is a fair -- there is a fair and rational inference on the evidence that Mr. Furundzija was not engaged in asking any questions in the pantry, and therefore, since that is the pivotal factual finding in the case, I would ask you to reverse that finding of the Trial Chamber. Ultimately, if the Prosecution were right, and that the Trial Chamber adhered to its own order and limited the evidence to what was charged in the indictment, we would have had a case as follows. And it's a point that I've reiterated. The issues in the case were: After Accused B had done what he had done in the large room, there are allegations by Witness A that she was interrogated and a knife was rubbed against her by a different person, who made another threat. There is nothing in the judgement that addresses that factual situation. There is no discussion of whether the rubbing of a knife coupled with an oral threat rises to extreme pain and suffering necessary for a conviction on torture. We submit that that is what those -- those are what the real issues in the case were. There is no answer to that question, and that is something else that you must resolve now. Our reading of the Tadic opinion, the first opinion in which a victim -- a fire extinguisher hose was placed in the mouth of a victim, and the Trial Chamber found that although there were threats made that the fire extinguisher was going to be discharged into the mouth of the victim, the Trial Chamber there came to the conclusion that it did not rise -- not only did not rise to torture, but it did not rise, I believe, to inhuman treatment. If my memory serves me correctly, I think that's the charge that they were addressing. The issues here, at least with respect to that portion in paragraph 25 of the rubbing of the knife, coupled with an oral threat, I don't -- or the Defence submits, do not rise to extreme pain and suffering as that term is defined in the first Tadic case. So what exactly are we asking the Appellate Chamber to do? We are asking you to do the following: to strike the findings of the Trial Chamber that are inconsistent with 25 and 26; that is, any factual finding that places Furundzija in the large room prior to Accused B's arrival should be stricken. Any findings in the large room that Mr. Furundzija questioned Witness A while -- and then subsequently Accused B rubbed the knife and made an oral threat, are clearly something that we were aware of and can be considered in the evidence. Taking the case further, it proceeds into the pantry. We are asking you to come to a finding that there was reasonable doubt as to whether or not Mr. Furundzija was engaged in asking questions in the pantry, to apply the standard that I've discussed already. Reading this testimony, reading his witness statement, which he gave two weeks or three weeks before trial, there is no doubt that he is saying, "Furundzija was not in the room." Given that, we believe that there is a fair and rational inference in the evidence of innocence, and it must be accepted on that issue. The fact -- again, to reiterate, in looking at the two witnesses, in order to defeat that testimony, we need overwhelming evidence that Witness D was wrong, and we don't have that in this case. We have two witnesses whose credibility was vouched for, and if one witness is to be believed over the other, then the Defence submits that it must be the witness whose credibility was impeached by anyone, and not the witness whose credibility was not impeached by the Defence, and whose testimony was stricken by the Trial Chamber because of its inconsistency with the indictment. As a matter of law, we think Witness D's testimony has to be accepted on this critical issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: I just want to -- excuse me. You made reference just now to the first Tadic case, where you said that the Chamber made a finding that it was not inhuman treatment or torture to place the water hose in the mouth of the victim. I may be wrong, but I recall in that particular case that finding was made on the basis that the victim was already dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's not consistent with my recollection, but I will be glad to go back to it and check it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: For the transcript, it was just Judge Vohrah who was asking the question, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We ask you, Your Honours -- sorry, and then finally to address --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I have the impression that you're winding up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would another five minutes be satisfactory to you, because one of our colleagues has to sit elsewhere. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm well aware of it, and I want to stay in your good graces. In summation, I've already outlined what we are asking you to do. At the very least, if you cannot acquit him, then we are asking for a new trial, a trial in which the facts of the case will be limited to the allegations in 25 and 26, and that Mr. Furundzija be given an opportunity to mount a defence as to what happened in the large room. We want fairness, we want a fair chance to defend Mr. Furundzija, and we don't believe we were given that fair chance, given all that transpired, both in the pre-trial stage and through those June 12 and June 15 hearings. And it cannot be said that we were put on notice that the large room was at issue in the trial. The very least level of assistance, and again it's one I hesitate to make, but I must, is that if you are going to affirm all of this and all of these issues, then let this be considered in mitigation of sentence. And much of what the Prosecution set out in its sentencing positions we agree with; however, there are certain aspects of it that we disagree with, including that, (A), the quality of the evidence in the case cannot be considered, at least in the jurisdiction that I practice in, the quality of the evidence is definitely something to be considered by the trier of fact in exercising its discretion on sentence. Second, again I reiterate Mr. Furundzija's relatively low level as parallel to the situation in the Tadic case on sentencing, and we ask for your assistance in reducing the harshness of this verdict. And again that is my extreme last-resort argument on appeal. I started off the day by telling you that you are the guardians of a right to a fair trial, and I started off by telling you that you have been charged to guard those provisions in the International Covenant and the European Convention and the Statute. We want a fair opportunity, and Mr. Furundzija has no one else to turn to but the five of you. We never were able to mount a defence on the issues that ultimately were seriously impacting upon the question of his guilt or innocence, and we did not get a resolution of our primary defence, which was Witness D's testimony; not so much as a paragraph saying: "Witness D says this, Witness A says that, we choose Witness A's version for the following reasons. And, Mr. Furundzija, if you disagree with how we have applied the standard of proof, you can take it to the Appeals Chamber." We don't even have that opportunity, because we don't know what the findings or what the reasoning was behind the decision not to consider Witness D's testimony. At the end of the day, if he is going to be convicted, we want a chance to defend him. When we try individuals in criminal cases, whether it's at the international level, or in Chicago, where I am from, but in particular in cases here involving war crimes, and where we allow the accused due process and a fair opportunity to defend himself, then regardless of the outcome, but even if the accused is convicted, we can all feel good that we have allowed the rule of law, ultimately, to condemn the defendant's conduct. However, where we convict a defendant and we did not afford him a fair opportunity to defend himself, then we have perpetuated injustice with more injustice. And we have condemned not the defendant, but ourselves to deal with the consequences. We put ourselves in your hands, and Mr. Furundzija puts himself in your hands to ensure that he gets a fair opportunity to defend himself. And we thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic, for your assistance, which we welcome. Perhaps there is one word which I may use in reply, and that is, if you felt it necessary, it was well within your rights to remind the Bench of the solemnity of its functions under the Statute to ensure a fair trial. All I would like to say to you, and this is by way of reassurance, is that the Bench is well aware of that responsibility, and the Bench hopes to [inaudible] it. So with those words, I would thank both sides for their assistance, and I would bring the proceedings today to an end. Yes, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I know the time frame. Just a couple of matters. As my friend has not withdrawn his claim that he raised in his appeal brief, the improper conviction of the appellant on Witness D, and our position is that it was -- it's not before you. If you feel inclined that it is before you, of course we reserve our right to file a response to that issue, as it was not in his appeal brief. If that's the position taken. I just wanted to put it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If necessary, I will take counsel with my colleagues about the necessity of issuing a Scheduling Order on that point. If necessary. But I doubt it. So, with those words, I bring the proceedings to an end. I thank both sides for their very fulsome and kindly assistance, which we welcome and value. Thank you. --- Adjourned at 5 p.m., sine die.
